senses.example: Antibodies bind to the pathogen, and the complement then helps destroy the invading bacteria.

senses.definition: An expression related to some other expression such that it is true under the same conditions that make other false, and vice versa.
senses.example: In logic, the complement of a proposition is true exactly when that proposition is false.

senses.definition: A voltage level with the opposite logical sense to the given one.
senses.example: The inverter's output sits at the complement of the input voltage level.

senses.definition: A bit with the opposite value to the given one; the logical complement of a number.
senses.example: Flip every bit to its complement by inverting the binary number before adding one.

senses.definition: A nucleotide sequence in which each base is replaced by the complementary base of the given sequence: adenine (A) by thymine (T) or uracil (U), cytosine (C) by guanine (G), and vice versa.
senses.example: A DNA molecule is formed from two strands, each of which is the complement of the other.

senses.definition: Synonym of alexin.
senses.example: Alexin was the name early researchers gave to what we now call complement.

senses.definition: Abbreviation of complementary good.
senses.example: Economists often treat printers and ink as a pair, each a complement to the other.

senses.definition: The whole working force of a vessel.
senses.example: The ship sailed with a complement of 300 officers and crew members aboard.

senses.definition: An interval which, together with the given interval, makes an octave.
senses.example: A perfect fifth is the musical complement of a perfect fourth within an octave.

senses.definition: (rare) Something (or someone) that completes; the consummation.
senses.example: Marriage was, for him, the complement of a lifetime spent searching for love.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To complete, to bring to perfection, to make whole.
senses.example: We believe your addition will complement the team.

senses.definition: To provide what the partner lacks and lack what the partner provides, thus forming part of a whole.
senses.example: The flavors of the pepper and garlic complement each other, giving a very rich taste in combination.

senses.definition: To change a voltage, number, color, etc. to its complement.
senses.example: The circuit complements the signal, changing each high voltage to low and vice versa.

core.definition: Something that completes something else or goes well with it, making a whole that is better or more complete.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, KAHM. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so say 'pluh' quickly, and do not confuse the noun with the verb, which is stressed on the last syllable of the root, KAHM-pluh-ment.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes things that improve or complete each other.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use complement in everyday talk about things that go well together, such as wine and food or a jacket and a scarf. Be careful: people often mix it up with compliment, which means praise, so the spelling and meaning must match. In math and technical talk, the word has specific senses that you will learn in those fields.

distinctions.note: A compliment is praise. A complement is something that completes or goes well with something else. Speakers often confuse them, so check the meaning.
A supplement is added to make up for a lack, often as an extra. A complement completes a whole that is already there, and it can be a natural partner.

examples.everyday: This white wine is a great complement to the salmon, so let's order a bottle.
examples.professional: The data engineer's skills are a strong complement to the analyst's modeling work on our team.
examples.analytical: Each virtue requires its complement, since humility without courage can slide into passivity.

nuance.analogy: Like a key and a lock, each one completing the other's purpose.
nuance.etymology: From Latin complementum, that which fills up or completes, from complere, to fill up.
common_mistakes: Writing or saying compliment when you mean complement, or the reverse.
Using complement as a verb with the noun stress pattern; the verb is pronounced KAHM-pluh-ment.

complement.etymology: From Middle English *complement*, from Latin *complēmentum* (“that which fills up or completes”), from *compleō* (“to fill up; to complete”) (English *complete*).

senses.definition: A (nonzero) natural number that is expressible as the product of two (or more) natural numbers other than itself and 1.
senses.example: Fifteen is a composite number because it equals three times five.

core.definition: A whole number greater than 1 that is not prime because it can be made by multiplying smaller whole numbers, such as 6 = 2 × 3.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAH in composite and on NUM in number. The -ite ending is a reduced 'it', not 'eet' or 'ot', and the final -er in number is a reduced American r sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans learn this term in middle and high school math and use it in classrooms, textbooks, and math discussions. Because the number 1 is neither prime nor composite, be careful when a class defines terms. In everyday talk, people usually just say that a number is composite or not prime.

distinctions.note: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself, while a composite number has at least one more factor.
Composite material in engineering means a material made from several different materials; composite number in math refers only to whole numbers with extra factors.

examples.everyday: My son said 9 is a composite number, and I had to look it up because I'd forgotten.
examples.professional: Before we run the algorithm, we should filter out composite numbers so the primality test only sees candidates.
examples.analytical: Every composite number n greater than 1 has a prime factor no greater than its square root, which is why trial division terminates quickly.

nuance.analogy: A composite number is like a LEGO model built from smaller bricks, while a prime is a single brick.
nuance.etymology: Composite comes from Latin compositus, 'put together', the past participle of componere.
common_mistakes: Counting 1 as a composite number, since it has only one factor and is therefore neither prime nor composite.
Confusing composite number with compound number, which is not a standard math term.

senses.definition: The settlement of differences by arbitration or by consent reached by mutual concessions.
senses.example: After weeks of negotiation, both sides accepted a compromise that gave each something important.

senses.definition: A committal to something derogatory or objectionable; a prejudicial concession; a surrender.
senses.example: a compromise of character or right

senses.definition: A breach of a computer or network's rules such that an unauthorized disclosure or loss of sensitive information may have occurred, or the unauthorized disclosure or loss itself.
senses.example: The security compromise exposed millions of customer records, and the company disclosed it only last week.

senses.definition: To bind by mutual agreement.
senses.example: Both parties were compromised by the agreement, binding them to its terms for ten years.

senses.definition: To adjust and settle by mutual concessions; to compound.
senses.example: The landlord and tenant agreed to compromise the dispute over the security deposit.

senses.definition: To find a way between extremes.
senses.example: Good leaders learn to compromise between their own ideals and what the team can realistically achieve.

senses.definition: To pledge by some act or declaration; to endanger the life, reputation, etc. of, by some act which can not be recalled; to expose to suspicion.
senses.example: By lying to the press, the senator compromised his reputation beyond repair.

senses.definition: To cause impairment of.
senses.example: Heavy smoke from the wildfire compromised the immune systems of nearby residents.

senses.definition: To illegally expose.
senses.example: The reporter refused to compromise the identity of her confidential source.

senses.definition: To breach (a security system).
senses.example: They tried to compromise the security in the computer by guessing the password.

core.definition: An agreement in which each side gives up some demands to reach a result that both can accept.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHM. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, so the word sounds like 'KAHM-pruh-myz'. Do not pronounce the second vowel as a full 'oh', and do not stress the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive. It suggests fairness, cooperation, and flexibility, though it can also imply giving up something important.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use compromise constantly in meetings, family arguments, and politics, as in 'Let's find a compromise.' A common reply is 'I can live with that' or 'Okay, let's meet halfway.' Saying 'I compromise' out loud can sound like you are giving in, so use it with some care.

distinctions.note: An agreement may be reached by one side winning. A compromise means both sides give something up.
A concession is one side giving something up, while a compromise involves a mutual exchange of concessions.

examples.everyday: We could not agree on a restaurant, so we found a compromise and picked the Thai place with the good noodles.
examples.professional: Let's propose a compromise: we ship the core feature on Friday, and the reporting module goes out the following sprint.
examples.analytical: A genuine compromise requires each party to revise its own priorities rather than merely trade demands on the table.

nuance.analogy: A compromise is like sharing a sidewalk: each person steps a little to the side so both can pass.
nuance.etymology: From Latin compromittere, meaning 'to promise together' or 'to agree mutually'.
common_mistakes: Using 'compromise with' and 'compromise about' interchangeably; the common pattern is 'reach a compromise with someone on something'.
Using the word to mean 'weakening' a principle in a negative sense without marking it, which can be confusing in serious discussions.
patterns: a compromise between A and B

compromise.etymology: From Middle French *compromis*, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin *compromissum* (“a compromise, originally a mutual promise to refer to arbitration”), prop.

conversation.text: Let's find a compromise that works for both teams.
As a compromise, we'll launch on time with fewer features.
We compromised on a two-week delay instead of a month.

senses.definition: The act of conceiving.
senses.example: Her conception of the project came during a long walk along the river.

senses.definition: The state of being conceived; the beginning.
The fertilization of an ovum by a sperm to form a zygote.
senses.example: Doctors explained that conception happens when a sperm fertilizes an egg in the fallopian tube.

senses.definition: The start of pregnancy.
senses.example: They tracked her cycle carefully, hoping for conception before the holidays.

senses.definition: The formation of a conceptus or an implanted embryo.
senses.example: The clinic monitored the embryo's development after conception and implantation in the uterine lining.

senses.definition: The power or faculty of apprehending of forming an idea in the mind; the power of recalling a past sensation or perception; the ability to form mental abstractions.
senses.example: Kant argued that human conception shapes how we perceive and organize experience.

senses.definition: An image, idea, or notion formed in the mind; a concept, plan or design.
senses.example: His conception of the ideal city included wide boulevards and public gardens everywhere.

senses.definition: Something conceived or designed.
senses.example: The architect's bold conception was a glass tower rising above the old harbor.

core.definition: The process of forming an idea or plan in the mind, or the moment an idea or project first takes shape.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEP, and the first syllable reduces to 'kun'. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun', never 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests creativity and the origin of something good.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conception mostly in formal writing, presentations, and reviews, especially in phrases like from conception to completion. In casual speech people usually say idea or start. Be careful in conversation because the word also has a biological meaning, so it can sound unexpected if you use it for a new project in a casual setting.

distinctions.note: A concept is the idea itself, while conception is the act or process of forming that idea.
Conception is forming an idea in the mind, while perception is taking in information through the senses or the understanding that results from it.

collocations: a clear conception of the goal
the conception of a new product

examples.everyday: The whole idea started at a barbecue, but the conception of the business didn't happen until my brother came up with the name.
examples.professional: From conception to launch, the project took eighteen months, and the team never changed its core goals.
examples.analytical: Descartes treats conception as the mind's clear grasp of an idea, prior to any judgment about whether that idea is true.

nuance.analogy: Like the moment a seed is planted in the soil, before anything visible has grown.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conceptio, from concipere 'to take in, conceive'.
common_mistakes: Using conception as a casual synonym for idea in everyday conversation, where idea sounds more natural
Confusing conception with concept, which is the idea itself rather than the act of forming it

conception.etymology: From Middle English *concepcioun*, borrowed from Old French *conception*, from Latin *conceptiō* (“a comprehending, a collection, composition, an expression, also a becoming pregnant”), from *concipiō*, past participle *conceptus* (“conceive”); see *conceive*.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or united in a confederacy.
senses.example: Confederate delegates met in Montgomery to draft a constitution in 1861.

senses.definition: Banded together; allied.
senses.example: The three neighborhood associations are confederate in their opposition to the new highway.

senses.definition: A member of a confederacy.
An accomplice in a plot.
An actor who participates in a psychological experiment pretending to be a subject but in actuality working for the researcher.
senses.example: The man posing as a fellow volunteer was a confederate of the researchers.

senses.definition: To unite persons or states in a league, confederacy or conspiracy; to ally, league.
senses.example: The rival clubs confederated to lobby the city council against the stadium plan.

core.definition: A member of a confederacy, or an accomplice who secretly helps someone with a plot or crime.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FED, and the final syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'ruht' rather than 'rate'. Do not confuse the noun pronunciation with the verb, which ends in 'rayt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a historical term, but negative when it means an accomplice in wrongdoing. Capitalized, Confederate has a painful association with the Civil War South.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, people usually say accomplice or partner in crime for someone who helps commit a wrong, and confederate sounds more formal or literary. In psychology, confederate is a standard term for a person secretly working with the researcher. Capitalized Confederate refers to the Civil War South and can be politically sensitive.

distinctions.note: Accomplice is the standard legal word for someone who helps commit a crime, while confederate is more formal and can also mean a research collaborator.
An ally is a supporter in a common cause, while a confederate is usually a member of a formal league or a secret helper in a plot.
Partner is neutral and everyday, while confederate often implies secrecy or a plot.

examples.everyday: My brother said his roommate was just a confederate in the prank, not the one who came up with it.
examples.professional: The study used a confederate who pretended to be another participant and gave the same scripted answers.
examples.analytical: The prosecutor argued that the defendant's confederate had shared the motive, which made the conspiracy charge stronger.

nuance.analogy: Like a teammate who passes the ball on cue in a magic trick, because the audience never sees the plan.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin confoederatus, 'united by league,' past participle of confoederare, 'to unite by treaty,' from com- and foedus 'league.'
common_mistakes: Using confederate as the everyday word for accomplice, when most Americans say accomplice or partner in crime.
Pronouncing the noun with the verb's ending 'rayt' instead of 'ruht'.
Capitalizing Confederate loosely, which can unintentionally signal the Civil War meaning.

confederate.etymology: in Middle english; Middle English *confederat* (“confederated, allied, associated in a plot; united or bound, as in friendship or troth”), borrowed from Late Latin *cōnfoederātus* perfect passive participle of *cōnfoederō*, see *-ate* and *-ate*.

senses.definition: To use one's authority to lay claim to and separate a possession from its holder.
senses.example: In schools, it is common for teachers to confiscate electronic games and other distractions.

core.definition: To officially take away someone's property, usually as a penalty or by legal authority, and keep it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress goes on the first syllable, KAHN, and the second syllable is a weak uh, so don't say 'fis.' The noun confiscation moves the stress to the -SKAY- syllable: kahn-fuh-SKAY-shun.

nuance.connotation: Negative or serious for the person losing property, but neutral when describing official procedure. Parents and teachers also use it casually.
nuance.usage_note: Police, airport security, and schools confiscate items, and parents informally say they 'confiscated' a phone. For a voluntary gift or a lost item, use take, take away, or hold. Formal news and legal texts favor confiscate, while everyday talk often uses take away.

distinctions.note: Seize is more forceful and often means grabbing something quickly, especially in police action. Confiscate implies an official taking, often with a rule or penalty behind it.
Take away is informal and general. Confiscate sounds official and suggests authority.

examples.everyday: The teacher confiscated my son's phone during class again.
examples.professional: Security confiscated two laptops at the gate, so plan on replacing one before the trip.
examples.analytical: Locke worried that a ruler who could confiscate property at will destroyed the security government was meant to protect.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee taking a player's card: the rule is clear, and the official removes the item.
nuance.etymology: From Latin confiscare 'to seize for the treasury', from com- 'together' + fiscus 'public treasury'.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on the second syllable (kun-FIS-kate); the first syllable carries the stress.
Using confiscate for something given away willingly or left behind; use take or pick up instead.

confiscate.etymology: Latin *cōnfiscātus*, the perfect passive participle of Latin *cōnfiscō* (“to seize for the public treasury (*fiscus*)”), see *-ate* and *-ate*.

senses.definition: To catch fire.
To set fire to something.

core.definition: To catch fire suddenly and burn fiercely, or to set something on fire in a large, destructive blaze.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHN. The middle syllable is a quick, reduced 'fluh,' not 'flag,' and the final syllable rhymes with 'great.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word describes destruction by fire, so it carries a sense of danger and loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'conflagrate' in everyday talk. You will mostly see it in news writing about large fires, in historical accounts, or in literary descriptions. In conversation, people say 'burn down,' 'go up in flames,' or 'catch fire.'

distinctions.note: 'Ignite' means to start burning, and it can be small and ordinary, like lighting a match. 'Conflagrate' implies a large, spreading, destructive fire.
'Burn' is the everyday word for fire damage or a flame's action. 'Conflagrate' is more formal and suggests a blaze that spreads out of control.

examples.professional: A faulty wire in the attic could conflagrate the whole roof before the smoke detector even goes off, so we need to replace it this week.
examples.analytical: Historians argue that the city's wooden architecture allowed a single spark to conflagrate entire neighborhoods within hours.

nuance.analogy: Like a match dropped into a pile of dry leaves, which quickly turns into a roaring bonfire.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conflagrare, 'to burn up completely,' from con- (together, thoroughly) and flagrare (to burn).
common_mistakes: Using 'conflagrate' for a small, ordinary fire. It is a strong word for a major blaze.
Confusing the verb 'conflagrate' with the noun 'conflagration,' which is the more common word in American writing.

conflagrate.etymology: Latin *cōnflāgrātus*, perfect passive participial of *cōnflāgrō* (“to be consumed by fire; to set aflame”), see *-ate*.

senses.definition: That which consists of many previously separate parts.
An instance of conglomerating, a coming together of separate parts.

core.definition: A group or mass made up of many separate things that have been joined or collected together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RAY, with a lighter stress on GLAH. The 'o' in 'glom' is the 'ah' sound of 'cot,' and the middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'muh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe a mixed collection positively or negatively, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'conglomeration' to describe a mixed collection of different things, such as styles, ideas, or buildings. In business, Americans say 'conglomerate' for a company that owns many different businesses, not 'conglomeration.' The word sounds formal, so in casual talk people often say 'a mix of' or 'a jumble of.'

distinctions.note: 'Conglomerate' is the more common word, especially for a company owning many businesses, while 'conglomeration' describes the general act or result of joining things together.
'Aggregation' is a more technical or statistical term for collecting data or units into a total, while 'conglomeration' describes a physical or social mixture.
'Mix' is informal and neutral, while 'conglomeration' is formal and suggests a varied group that has come together.

examples.everyday: Her living room is a strange conglomeration of antiques, sports posters, and handmade pottery.
examples.professional: The report describes the product line as a conglomeration of tools built by different acquisitions over ten years.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the modern university is a conglomeration of departments with competing purposes rather than a single institution.

nuance.analogy: A conglomeration is like a potluck table where many separate dishes are placed together to make one large meal.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conglomerare, meaning 'to wind into a ball,' from con- and glomus, meaning 'ball'.
common_mistakes: Calling a company a 'conglomeration' rather than a 'conglomerate,' which is the standard business term.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying kun-GLOM-er-AY-shun instead of kun-glah-muh-RAY-shun.

senses.definition: Joined together in pairs.
senses.example: The engineers twisted the wires in conjugated pairs to reduce electrical interference in the cable.

senses.definition: Containing one or more pairs of double bonds and/or lone pairs, each pair being separated by a single bond.
senses.example: The chemist explained that the conjugated diene system stabilizes the molecule through delocalized electrons.

core.definition: In chemistry, describing a molecule with alternating single and double bonds, letting electrons spread across several atoms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, CON-, and keep the middle syllables short and reduced. The final -ed is pronounced as its own syllable, /ɪd/, in this chemistry sense, not as a silent or simple /t/ ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American chemistry classes, labs and research papers, conjugated describes a bonding pattern, not a verb form. You will see it in organic chemistry, biochemistry and materials science, often with words like 'system' or 'double bonds'. The grammatical past participle of 'conjugate' is a different use of the same word.

distinctions.note: Isolated double bonds are separated by two or more single bonds, while conjugated double bonds are separated by only one single bond.
The verb form is used for grammar and for chemical pairs, while the adjective conjugated in chemistry describes bonding and electron sharing.

examples.everyday: My chemistry tutor said the bright color in this dye comes from a conjugated system of bonds.
examples.professional: The drug's activity depends on a conjugated system, so we changed the ring structure in the lab to improve its stability.
examples.analytical: The conjugated system delocalizes electrons across several atoms, which lowers the molecule's energy and shifts its absorption spectrum.

nuance.analogy: A conjugated system is like a shared ride-share lane: electrons can move freely across several lanes instead of staying in one.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conjugare 'to join together', via the verb conjugate.
common_mistakes: Saying 'con-ju-GAY-ted' with the stress on the wrong syllable.
Confusing the chemistry adjective with the grammatical sense of conjugated verbs.

conjugated.etymology: Inflected form of *conjugate*. *konjugieren*, coined 1899 by German chemist Johannes Thiele.

senses.definition: Related by birth or "by blood", i.e. having close ancestors in common.
A person related to another by birth.

core.definition: Related by blood, meaning sharing a common ancestor; a term used mainly in legal, genealogical, or historical writing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAHN, with a weaker secondary stress on -sang. The middle -ng- is a true ng sound, and the final -ine is pronounced 'in'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is used in genealogy, law, or historical writing and can sound pompous in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans seldom use consanguine in everyday talk; they say 'blood relative' or 'related by blood.' You will see it in legal documents about marriage laws, inheritance, or genealogy, and in older texts. In casual conversation, 'family' or 'blood relative' sounds natural.

distinctions.note: Consanguineous is the more common adjective; consanguine is rarer and more literary or archaic.
Affine refers to relation by marriage in legal or anthropological terms, while consanguine refers to relation by blood.

examples.professional: The genealogy database flags consanguine matches between donors, which matters for medical screening.
examples.analytical: The statute restricts marriage between persons in certain consanguine relationships, drawing lines by descent rather than affection.

nuance.analogy: Consanguine is like a family tree drawn in ink: it records the lines of blood that connect people.
nuance.etymology: From Latin consanguineus, from con- 'together' and sanguis 'blood'.
common_mistakes: Using consanguine as an everyday word, when blood relative is more natural.
Confusing consanguine with affine, which refers to relation by marriage.

senses.definition: That may be construed.
senses.example: The contract's vague clause was construable in two ways, which is why the lawyers kept arguing about it.

core.definition: Able to be interpreted or understood in a particular way, especially as a meaning or intention.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'stroo', the second syllable. The ending '-able' is reduced to 'uh-bul', and the r should be clearly American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes possible interpretations, often in legal or academic writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in legal, academic and formal writing, usually in the phrase 'can be construed as'. In everyday speech, people say 'could be taken as' or 'could be read as'. The adjective itself is less common than the verb 'construe' in actual use.

distinctions.note: Understandable means easy to comprehend; construable means it can be interpreted in a particular way, which may be unclear.
Ambiguous means having more than one possible meaning; construable is about being interpreted in a way that can be defended.

examples.everyday: Her joke is construable as sarcasm, so don't take it too seriously.
examples.professional: The clause is construable in two ways, so legal will need to clarify the scope before we sign.
examples.analytical: The passage is construable as a metaphor, but the grammar points toward a literal reading.

nuance.analogy: A construable sentence is like a door with two keys; both can open it, so you must choose which one fits the context.
nuance.etymology: From the verb construe, from Latin construere, 'to pile up, put together'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'construable' with 'constructible', which means able to be built.
Using 'construable' as a verb; the verb is 'construe'.

senses.definition: To look at on all sides or in all its aspects; to view or consider with continued attention; to regard with deliberate care; to meditate on; to study, ponder, or consider.
senses.example: Each night she sat by the window and contemplated the meaning of her grandmother's last letter.

senses.definition: To consider as a possibility.
senses.example: I contemplated doing the project myself, but it would have taken too long.

core.definition: To think carefully and at length about something, or to consider doing it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHN, in American speech. The middle syllables are weak, so avoid giving them full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it suggests serious thought, often before a decision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I'm contemplating...' to mean they are seriously thinking about a choice, such as moving or changing jobs. It is more formal than 'think about' and can sound stiff in very casual talk. A natural reply is 'Good luck with that' or 'What's making you think about it?'

distinctions.note: Consider is more common and neutral, while contemplate suggests longer, deeper thought.
Ponder suggests quiet, puzzled thinking, while contemplate can be about a decision or a big idea.

examples.everyday: I'm contemplating a move to Denver, but I haven't decided yet.
examples.professional: Leadership is contemplating a move to the new data platform next quarter, so please share your concerns.
examples.analytical: Descartes asks us to contemplate the nature of the mind apart from the body, which he thinks reveals certain truths.

nuance.analogy: To contemplate something is like turning a stone over in your hand, looking at it from every side before deciding what it is.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contemplari, to observe, consider, from templum, a space marked out for observation.
common_mistakes: Using 'contemplate' with 'about' as in 'contemplate about', which is not standard.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'kun-TEM-plate'.

contemplate.etymology: Latin *contemplātus*, the perfect active participle of *contemplor* (“to observe, survey, gaze, contemplate”), see *-ate*.

senses.definition: Someone who competes with one or more other people.
senses.example: Three contenders are running for the open seat on the city council this fall.

senses.definition: Someone who has a viable chance of winning a competition.

core.definition: A person, team, or company that has a real chance of winning a competition, election, or contract.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the second syllable, TEN. The final -er is an unstressed r-colored syllable, so say 'dur' lightly, not as a full 'dehr'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests strength, skill, and a real chance to win.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contender a lot in sports, politics, and business. Phrases like 'a serious contender' or 'a top contender' are very common in sports talk and news. You might say to a friend, 'They're a real contender this year.' A natural reply is 'I hope so.'

distinctions.note: A competitor is anyone who takes part in a contest; a contender is someone with a real chance of winning.
A candidate is someone nominated for a job or election; a contender is someone who is seen as likely to win.
A challenger tries to take a title or position from its current holder; a contender may be competing for an open prize.

examples.everyday: The Cardinals are a real contender this year, so I'm going to buy tickets for the playoffs.
examples.professional: Our vendor is a strong contender for the contract, but the security review is still open, so we can't decide yet.
examples.analytical: Among theories of consciousness, global workspace theory is the strongest contender for explaining how information becomes available to experience.

nuance.analogy: A contender is like a runner who is close behind the leader in the final lap: still in the race, with a real chance to win.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contendere, 'to strive, contend'.
common_mistakes: Using contender for someone who simply takes part in a contest; use competitor or participant for that.
Using the preposition 'to' instead of 'for', as in 'a contender to the title' rather than 'a contender for the title'.

senses.definition: Arranged by contract; established by agreement.
Made smaller by contraction.
senses.example: The doctor noticed the contracted muscle in her calf after the long run.

senses.definition: Incurred; acquired.
senses.example: He contracted a large debt when he financed the used car.

core.definition: Bound or arranged by a contract, such as a contracted employee, contracted work, or a contracted rate.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TRAK. The final -ed is pronounced as a separate syllable, 'tid', because it follows the t sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It simply describes an arrangement, with no positive or negative implication.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'contracted' mostly for work arrangements, like 'contracted services' or 'contracted staff.' In speech, 'I'm contracted' sounds stiff, so people say 'I work under a contract' or 'I'm on contract.' In grammar, teachers also say 'contracted form' for words like 'don't.'

distinctions.note: Contracted describes something that has been arranged by a contract; contractual describes what is required by or related to a contract.
Contracting is an activity, such as 'government contracting'; contracted describes a state or arrangement.

examples.everyday: My cousin is contracted with a cell tower company, so he travels a lot for work.
examples.professional: We have three contracted developers on the project through the end of the quarter.
examples.analytical: A contracted workforce complicates labor law, since obligations depend on the specific terms of each agreement.

nuance.analogy: A contracted worker is like a guest who is invited for a specific visit, with the terms of the visit written down in advance.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of contract, from Latin contrahere, 'to draw together.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am contracted' when you mean you have a job agreement; 'I'm on contract' sounds more natural.
Confusing 'contracted' (bound by agreement) with 'contracted' (shortened) in the grammar sense.

senses.definition: One of a pair of propositions that cannot both be simultaneously true, though they may both be false.
senses.example: In logic, the contrary of 'all swans are white' is 'no swans are white.'

senses.definition: The opposite.
senses.example: Everyone expected him to quit, but he did the contrary and stayed.

senses.definition: (historical) A type of loaded die.
senses.example: The gambler was caught using a contrary die that always landed on six.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Opposite; in an opposite direction; in opposition; adverse.
senses.example: contrary winds

senses.definition: Opposed; contradictory; inconsistent.
senses.example: Her contrary opinions made every committee meeting longer than it needed to be.

senses.definition: Given to opposition; perverse; wayward.
senses.example: a contrary disposition; a contrary child

senses.definition: Contrarily.
senses.example: I never act contrary to my principles.

core.definition: Opposed to something, or going in the opposite direction; not in agreement with what is expected or stated.

pronunciation.tip: In the phrase 'contrary to,' the stress is on the second syllable, TRAIR. In the phrases 'on the contrary' and 'a contrary person,' Americans stress the first syllable, KAHN-trair-ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the sense of opposed or inconsistent; mildly negative when describing a person who is perverse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'contrary to' in writing and speech to say something goes against a rule, belief, or expectation, as in 'contrary to popular belief.' 'On the contrary' is a common spoken response that firmly corrects someone. Describing a person as contrary means they are stubborn or argumentative, which is a mild criticism. In casual talk, 'the opposite' is often more natural.

distinctions.note: Opposite describes a direct reversal, while contrary can describe something that conflicts with a rule or expectation without being its exact reverse.
Contradictory describes statements that cannot both be true; contrary can describe actions, opinions, or situations that conflict in a broader sense.

examples.everyday: Contrary to what my dad said, the store is actually open on Sundays, so we can go after church.
examples.professional: Contrary to our forecast, customer churn increased last quarter, so we need to revisit the model.
examples.analytical: Contrary to the classical view, the argument suggests that virtue cannot be separated from the conditions in which it is practiced.

nuance.analogy: Like walking into a headwind when everyone else is pushed forward by the wind at their back.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contrarius, opposite, from contra, against.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable: 'on the CONtrary' is correct, but 'contrary to' is stressed on TRAIR.
Using 'contrary' as a noun for 'opposite' in everyday speech, where 'the opposite' is more natural.

contrary.etymology: From Middle English *contrarie*, compare, from Old French *contraire*, from Latin *contrārius* (“opposite, opposed, contrary”), from *contrā* (“against”).

senses.definition: The reversal of the order of data types acted upon by an operator.
A functor which reverses composition.
Of vectors, the property of scaling inversely with a change of basis, as opposed to covariance.

core.definition: In type theory and category theory, a reversal of direction in a type relation, so that mappings flow opposite to covariance.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on VAIR, the stressed syllable of 'variance', with a secondary stress on KON. The final syllables are reduced to 'ee-uns', and the 'ar' sound is a clean r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Mainly computer scientists, programming-language designers, and mathematicians use this word, usually when discussing how function types or type parameters can be substituted. Most people never encounter it outside those fields. Americans stress it the same way they stress 'variance'.

distinctions.note: Covariance means the type or transformation changes in the same direction as the input, while contravariance changes in the opposite direction.
In statistics variance measures spread; contravariance is a specific directional behavior in typing or vector transformation and shares only the root.
Bivariance means a relation can be treated as either covariant or contravariant, and it is much less common than the other two.

examples.everyday: My friend who codes in Scala tried to explain contravariance over coffee, and I just nodded.
examples.professional: The compiler rejects the override because the parameter type needs contravariance, not covariance.
examples.analytical: Contravariance in the argument position preserves substitutability, since a function accepting a broader type can safely replace one accepting a narrower type.

nuance.analogy: Like a shadow that moves in the opposite direction to the object casting it.
nuance.etymology: From contra- 'against' plus variance, from Latin variare 'to vary'.
common_mistakes: Confusing contravariance with covariance, which is the same-direction relation.
Putting the main stress on the first syllable instead of VAIR.

senses.definition: A (mechanical) device to perform a certain task.
A means, such as an elaborate plan or strategy, to accomplish a certain objective.
senses.example: The negotiators devised a contrivance to get both parties to sign without admitting defeat.

senses.definition: Something overly artful or artificial.
senses.example: The novel's coincidences felt like a contrivance, arranged only to make the ending work.

senses.definition: The making of cunning or deceitful plans.
senses.example: The con artist's contrivance involved forged letters and a fake bank account.

core.definition: A device or a clever arrangement built to perform a particular task, or a plan designed to get a result, sometimes in a sneaky way.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on TRY, and the final -ance is a weak, unstressed 'uns.' Do not stress the last syllable, and do not pronounce the v as a b or f.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when it names a device, but negative when it suggests a trick or artificial scheme. Context shows which meaning applies.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, a device is more often called a gadget, tool or contraption. Contrivance is more formal and often used in writing, for example for a clever mechanism or for a plot that feels artificial. Calling a plan or story a contrivance usually suggests it is too forced or staged.

distinctions.note: Contraption is informal and often humorous for a strange or odd device, while contrivance is more formal and can refer to a clever mechanism or an artificial plan.
Device is neutral and common for any tool or mechanism; contrivance suggests ingenuity or artificiality, and it is less common in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: My grandfather built a little contrivance out of old bike parts to open the garage door without getting out of the truck.
examples.professional: The team's dashboard was a clever contrivance for tracking deployments, but nobody else understood how it worked.
examples.analytical: Critics argued that the plot's coincidences were a contrivance designed to rescue the hero rather than to reveal character.

nuance.analogy: A contrivance is like a stage set: it may work very well, but it looks built rather than natural.
nuance.etymology: From contrive, from Old French controver, 'to invent,' plus the English suffix -ance.
common_mistakes: Using contrivance for any ordinary tool; use tool or device for everyday objects.
Pronouncing the stress on the last syllable, as in kuhn-try-VANCE.

senses.definition: One who regularly engages in public controversies.
senses.example: Richard Dawkins has become a leading controversialist in a few areas.

core.definition: A person who regularly takes part in public arguments or debates, often defending a position strongly against opponents.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'VUR', the third syllable, and the 'er' in the middle is a rhotic vowel. Non-native speakers often stress 'CON' or say 'vair' for the middle syllable; the American pronunciation is 'vur'.

nuance.connotation: Often negative: it suggests someone who enjoys conflict or argument for its own sake.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. They would more likely say 'he loves to argue' or 'she's a provocative debater'. In formal writing or history it describes someone who writes or speaks to provoke public disputes. Calling someone a controversialist can sound like a mild insult.

distinctions.note: A debater takes part in structured arguments, often in a set format, while a controversialist engages in public disputes more freely and often aggressively.
A polemicist writes hostile attacks on opposing views, while a controversialist may speak or write and is defined by taking part in public disputes.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a real controversialist; he'll argue with anybody at Thanksgiving dinner.
examples.professional: The conference invited a well-known controversialist to speak, which created tension among the sponsors.
examples.analytical: As a controversialist, the pamphleteer wrote to provoke, and his aim was to win the argument rather than to clarify the truth.

nuance.analogy: A controversialist is like a boxer who looks for a fight at every press conference, whether or not the match is worth it.
nuance.etymology: From controversy, from Latin controversia, 'dispute', from contra, 'against', and vertere, 'to turn'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable 'KAHN-truh-vur-shuh-list'; the stress falls on the third syllable.
Using 'controversialist' when 'controversial' (an adjective) is needed, as in 'a controversial figure'.

senses.definition: A debate or discussion of opposing opinions; strife.
senses.example: The mayor's decision to close the library sparked a fierce controversy across town.

core.definition: A prolonged, often heated public disagreement among people who hold opposing opinions about an issue.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, KON, not on the middle syllable. The second syllable reduces to a weak 'truh' and the last to 'see'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It implies conflict and public heat, so it sounds unpleasant when you describe a dispute, but it can be neutral when you simply report that a debate exists.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'controversy' for public disputes in news, politics, science, and schools, such as a controversy over a city budget or a new vaccine. In casual talk people often say 'a big fuss' or 'drama,' but 'controversy' is standard in print and in serious conversation. You will often hear 'without controversy' or 'there's some controversy about' in news reports.

distinctions.note: A dispute is usually a conflict between particular parties over a claim, a contract, or a right, while a controversy is a broader public debate involving many people.
A debate is often structured and neutral, with an explicit format, while a controversy suggests tension and public disagreement without rules.
An argument is usually personal and informal, while a controversy is public and attracts wider attention.

examples.everyday: I didn't know the new park was such a controversy until I saw the neighborhood meeting on the news.
examples.professional: The leadership team wants to avoid another controversy, so we should prepare a clear statement before the press release goes out.
examples.analytical: The controversy over the historical sources reveals deeper disagreements about what counts as evidence.

nuance.analogy: A controversy is like a pot being stirred: once someone starts it, everyone nearby gets pulled into the mix.
nuance.etymology: From Latin controversia, 'dispute, debate,' from contra 'against' plus vertere 'to turn.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'controversy about' in some contexts where 'over' or 'surrounding' sounds more natural, for example 'the controversy over the law' rather than 'the controversy of the law.'
Using 'controversy' as a countable noun without an article in phrases like 'a controversy' versus 'much controversy,' where it is uncountable.
Stressing the second syllable (con-TRO-versy) instead of the first.

controversy.etymology: From Middle English *controversie*, from Old French *controversie*, from Latin *contrōversia* (“debate, contention, controversy”), from *contrōversus* (“turned in an opposite direction”).

senses.definition: In AI: The point in training where the loss stops improving meaningfully.
senses.example: Training stopped once the validation loss reached convergence and no longer improved meaningfully.

senses.definition: The process or property of approaching some limiting value; typically of an infinite series.
The act of moving toward union or uniformity.
senses.example: The two political parties showed convergence on tax policy after years of bitter disagreement.

senses.definition: A meeting place.
senses.example: We built a homestead at the convergence of two rivers

senses.definition: The intersection of three electron beams for red, green and blue onto a single pixel in a CRT.
senses.example: Shadow mask monitors achieve sharp color by aligning the convergence of the three electron beams.

senses.definition: The hypothesis that poorer economies' per capita incomes tend to grow faster than richer economies.
senses.example: Economists debated convergence, testing whether poor countries really catch up to rich ones over time.

senses.definition: The merging of distinct technologies, industries, or devices into a unified whole.
senses.example: Convergence of phone, camera, and music player into one device changed how we communicate.

senses.definition: A zone where two prevailing wind flows meet and interact, resulting in distinctive weather conditions.
senses.example: Heavy storms formed along the convergence zone where the sea breeze met the inland wind.

senses.definition: The coordinated focusing of the eyes, especially at short range.
senses.example: The optometrist tested his convergence at close range to check for double vision.

senses.definition: The evolution of similar structures or traits in unrelated species in similar environments; convergent evolution.
senses.example: Dolphins and sharks show convergence in body shape, despite evolving from very different ancestors.

core.definition: The process of approaching a stable limiting value, such as a training loss or a mathematical series, rather than diverging.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VUR, and the 'g' is pronounced /dʒ/ as in 'judge'. The final -ence is reduced to 'uhns'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral: in engineering it means the process is working, and in general use it means things coming together.
nuance.usage_note: In data science and AI, people talk about a model reaching convergence, meaning its loss has stopped improving meaningfully. In everyday English, it describes ideas, interests or places coming together. Americans say 'the model converged' as a verb more often than the noun form.

distinctions.note: Divergence means moving apart or failing to approach a limit; convergence means approaching a common point or limit.
Consensus is agreement among people; convergence can describe values, methods or numbers moving toward the same result.

examples.everyday: We had different ideas at first, but by the end of dinner there was real convergence on the plan.
examples.professional: We stop training once validation loss shows convergence, usually after about fifty epochs.
examples.analytical: The proof establishes convergence in probability, which is weaker than almost sure convergence but enough for the estimator to be consistent.

nuance.analogy: Like a ball rolling into the bottom of a bowl: it keeps moving until it settles near the lowest point.
nuance.etymology: From Latin convergere, to incline together.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'con-ver-jence' with a hard g instead of the /dʒ/ sound
Using convergence to mean agreement between people only, when it also describes numbers and processes

conversation.text: We stopped at convergence, once the training loss had been flat for several thousand steps.
With a suitable learning rate, convergence to a global minimum is guaranteed for convex problems but not for neural networks.
There's a convergence of opinion on the team that we should simplify the pipeline.

senses.definition: A firmly held belief.
A judgment of guilt in a court of law.
senses.example: His conviction for fraud meant he could no longer work as an accountant.

senses.definition: The state of being wholly convinced.
The state of being found or proved guilty.

core.definition: A firmly held belief or opinion, or a strong sense that something is true, often connected with your values.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VIK. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun,' and the middle vowel in the first syllable is a short 'i,' not 'ee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests strength of character, though a 'conviction' can also be stubborn in a negative sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I have a conviction that...' or 'she spoke with conviction' for firm beliefs. In legal contexts, a 'conviction' is a judgment of guilt, as in 'a conviction for fraud.' People say 'deeply held convictions' for strong moral or religious beliefs, which is common in political and public speech.

distinctions.note: Belief is a general word for thinking something is true; conviction is stronger and more emotionally held.
An opinion can be weak or changeable; a conviction is firmly held and often tied to your values.
Persuasion is the process of changing someone's mind; conviction is the state of being firmly convinced.

examples.everyday: She spoke with real conviction about her hometown's new library, and it made me want to visit.
examples.professional: I have a strong conviction that our churn problem is in onboarding, not pricing, so let's test that first.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard distinguishes objective certainty from the inward conviction of faith, which he holds with passionate subjectivity.

nuance.analogy: Like a keel on a boat: it keeps you steady when the wind of other opinions pushes against you.
nuance.etymology: From Latin convictio, 'proof or refutation,' from convincere, 'to overcome by argument.'
common_mistakes: Using conviction to mean a mild opinion; for a light view, say 'I think' or 'my opinion.'
Confusing the legal sense (a judgment of guilt) with the sense of firm belief.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word elenchos in Hebrews 11:1 (RSV) is translated 'conviction,' meaning proof or inward certainty about things not seen. John 16:8 uses the related verb elenchō, meaning to convict or expose, to describe the Spirit's work of showing the world its sin. Romans 14:5 (RSV) says each person should be fully convinced in his own mind, from the Greek plērophoreō, meaning to be fully assured.

conviction.etymology: From late Middle English *conviction*, from Anglo-Norman *conviction*, from Latin *convictiō*, from *convictus*, the past participle of *convincō* (“to convict”).

senses.definition: The act of coordinating, making different people or things work together for a goal or effect.
senses.example: Coordination of the relief effort required daily calls between three separate agencies.

senses.definition: The resulting state of working together; cooperation; synchronization.
senses.example: Good coordination between the nurses and surgeons kept the operating room running smoothly.

senses.definition: The ability to coordinate one's senses and physical movements in order to act skillfully.
senses.example: I’m terrible at sports; I have no coordination.

senses.definition: The state of being equal in rank or power.
An equal joining together of two or more phrases or clauses, for example, using and, or, or but.
senses.example: The grammar lesson covered coordination and subordination, which confused several students at first.

senses.definition: The reaction of one or more ligands with a metal ion to form a coordination compound.
senses.example: The chemist studied the coordination of water molecules around the copper ion.

core.definition: The process of organizing people or activities so they work together smoothly toward a goal, or the body's ability to control movements.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on NAY, and the 'ti' is pronounced 'shun'. The first syllable has a secondary stress, so say 'koh-or-dih' with a lighter emphasis.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes organized effort and skill.
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces, coordination often refers to planning among teams, such as 'Her coordination of the event was excellent.' It is also used for physical skill, like 'hand-eye coordination.' In casual talk, Americans may say 'working together' or 'getting everyone on the same page' instead.

distinctions.note: Cooperation focuses on willingness to help; coordination focuses on arranging the timing and roles of people or actions.
Organization is the structure of a group; coordination is the active process of making its parts work together.

examples.everyday: Her hand-eye coordination is great, so she's a natural at tennis.
examples.professional: Good coordination between the design and engineering teams will keep the launch on schedule.
examples.analytical: Coordination among independent agents raises the question of how shared goals emerge without central command.

nuance.analogy: Coordination is like a relay race: each runner must be ready at the exact moment the baton is passed.
nuance.etymology: From coordinate, with the suffix -ion.
common_mistakes: Saying 'coordination with' and then forgetting the object; the usual phrase is 'coordination between' two groups.
Placing stress on the first syllable, as in 'COH-ordination'; the main stress is on NAY.

coordination.etymology: From Middle French *coordination*, from Late Latin *coōrdinātiōnem* (accusative of *coōrdinātiō*), from *con-* + *ōrdinātiō*.

senses.definition: Of or relating to Corinth.
Elaborate, ornate.
Debauched in character or practice; impure.
senses.example: The preacher condemned the Corinthian excess of the city's wealthy, calling it a shame.

senses.definition: Being a sporting event (originally in horse racing and yachting) restricted to gentleman amateurs.
senses.example: The Corinthian regatta was restricted to amateur sailors who had never accepted prize money.

senses.definition: Of the Corinthian order.
An inhabitant or a resident of Corinth, and its suburbs.
senses.example: The Corinthian merchant sold olive oil and pottery to traders from across the Aegean.

senses.definition: An inhabitant, a resident of; a thing that originates from Corinthia.
senses.example: The Corinthian wine in the cellar came from vineyards in the Peloponnese hills.

senses.definition: An accomplished amateur athlete.
senses.example: The Corinthian runner competed for the love of the sport and never sought any prize money.

senses.definition: A sailboat owner who helms their own boat in competitive racing.
senses.example: The Corinthian sailor steered his own wooden boat through the regatta without hiring a professional crew.

senses.definition: A worldly, fashionable person, accepted in society though possibly dissolute.
senses.example: The Corinthian in the regency novel dined with dukes yet gambled away fortunes nightly.

core.definition: Relating to the ancient Greek city of Corinth; in architecture, describing the most ornate of the classical column styles.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'IN', the second syllable. The 'th' is voiceless, as in 'thin', and the ending 'ian' is an unstressed 'ee-un'. Do not say 'core-in-thee-an'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when it describes architecture or the city; positive when it means ornate or luxurious.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'Corinthian' is mainly heard in architecture, art history and Bible study. Many Americans know it from 'Corinthian columns' on banks and courthouses. The city name is pronounced 'KOR-inth', and the adjective is 'ker-IN-thee-un'. Avoid using it casually to mean 'wild' or 'debauched', which is outdated.

distinctions.note: Doric is the plainest classical column style with a simple capital; Corinthian is the most decorated.
Ionic columns have scroll-shaped volutes on the capital; Corinthian capitals are covered in acanthus leaves.
Corinth is the city name; Corinthian is the adjective describing things from it or the style named after it.

examples.everyday: The old bank downtown has big Corinthian columns out front, so the building looks very formal.
examples.professional: The restoration plan keeps the Corinthian capitals, since they are the building's most original feature.
examples.analytical: Paul's letters to the Corinthian church respond to specific disputes within a congregation shaped by Greek urban culture.

nuance.analogy: Like the most decorated version of a column, with a top that looks like a bouquet of leaves.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Corinthius, from Greek Korinthios, from Korinthos, the name of the city of Corinth.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable incorrectly, as in 'core-IN-thee-un' with the stress on 'core'.
Confusing the adjective Corinthian with the city name Corinth, which is pronounced 'KOR-inth'.
nuance.biblical_note: Corinth was a major Greek port city where Paul preached and founded a church, described in Acts 18:1-18. Paul wrote to the church there, and 1 Corinthians 1:2 addresses 'the church of God which is at Corinth'. 1 Corinthians 13 is the famous chapter on love. The Greek name is Korinthos.

senses.definition: One who corrects.
senses.example: Our copy editor is a careful corrector who catches every stray comma in the manuscript.

core.definition: A person or thing that fixes errors, faults, or defects in writing, data, or equipment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KOR, and the final -or is a weak schwa sound. The r after the vowel is pronounced in American speech, so avoid a British-style dropped r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a role or tool for fixing problems, with no negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use corrector mainly in technical or editorial contexts, such as a color corrector in photography or a lens corrector in optics. In publishing, people more often say copy editor or proofreader. In everyday speech, a person who points out errors might be called a stickler or someone who always corrects you.

distinctions.note: An editor improves the content and structure of a whole text, while a corrector focuses on fixing specific errors.
A proofreader checks the final typeset version for typos and formatting, while a corrector can work at any stage to fix errors.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was the family corrector, always quick to fix anyone's grammar at dinner.
examples.professional: Our publisher hired a freelance corrector to catch errors before the manuscript goes to print.
examples.analytical: The critic becomes a corrector of the tradition when he exposes errors that its defenders have long overlooked.

nuance.analogy: A corrector is like a proofreader's red pen: it finds the mistakes and marks them so they can be fixed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin corrector, from corrigere 'to make straight, to set right'.
common_mistakes: Using corrector when you mean the act of correcting, which is correction.
Pronouncing the first syllable as KOR-rect-or, adding extra syllables.

senses.definition: In a covert manner, secretly.
senses.example: The agents covertly photographed the meeting from a van across the street.

core.definition: In a secret way, so that others do not notice or know what is happening.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, VURT, with an r-colored vowel. Many learners stress the first syllable, but the -ly ending is a clear 'lee.'

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, depending on context. It often suggests deception, espionage, or something done to avoid scrutiny, but it can describe harmless secrecy too.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use covertly most often in news, politics, intelligence, and business reporting, where it suggests a planned effort to stay hidden. In ordinary conversation people more often say secretly or on the sly. It is not usually used for small private matters like sneaking a snack.

distinctions.note: Secretly is the common everyday word, while covertly suggests a more deliberate or strategic concealment, often by an organization or agent.
Surreptitiously is more formal and emphasizes stealth or sneaking, often in a small, quick action.
Openly is the opposite; it means done publicly with nothing hidden.

examples.everyday: She covertly checked her phone under the table while her boss was talking.
examples.professional: A competitor covertly tested our pricing with fake accounts, so we have tightened the login checks.
examples.analytical: The regime covertly funded opposition groups while publicly denying any interference in the election.

nuance.analogy: Covertly is like a lantern turned down low: the light is there, but it is hidden from most of the room.
nuance.etymology: From covert (adjective), from Old French covert, past participle of covrir (to cover), plus -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (KOH-vert-lee) instead of the second.
Confusing covert with overt, which means open and obvious.
Using covertly for a trivial action where secretly is more natural.

senses.definition: To form cracks.
senses.example: It's been so dry, the ground is starting to crack.

senses.definition: To break apart under force, stress, or pressure.
senses.example: When I tried to stand on the chair, it cracked.

senses.definition: To become debilitated by psychological pressure.
senses.example: Anyone would crack after being hounded like that.

senses.definition: To break down or yield, especially under interrogation or torture.
senses.example: When we showed him the pictures of the murder scene, he cracked.

senses.definition: To make a cracking sound.
senses.example: The bat cracked with authority and the ball went for six.

senses.definition: To change rapidly in register.
senses.example: His voice cracked with emotion.

senses.definition: To alternate between high and low register in the process of eventually lowering.
senses.example: His voice finally cracked when he was fourteen.

senses.definition: To make a sharply humorous comment.
senses.example: "I would too, with a face like that," she cracked.

senses.definition: To realize that one is transgender.
senses.example: She cracked at age 22 and came out to her friends and family over the next few months.

senses.definition: To make a crack or cracks in.
senses.example: The ball cracked the window.

senses.definition: To break open or crush to small pieces by impact or stress.
senses.example: You'll need a hammer to crack a black walnut.

senses.definition: To strike forcefully.
senses.example: She cracked him over the head with her handbag.

senses.definition: To open slightly.
senses.example: Could you please crack the window?

senses.definition: To cause to yield under interrogation or other pressure.
senses.example: They managed to crack him on the third day.

senses.definition: To solve a difficult problem.
senses.example: I've finally cracked it, and of course the answer is obvious in hindsight.

senses.definition: To overcome a security system or component.
senses.example: It took a minute to crack the lock, three minutes to crack the security system, and about twenty minutes to crack the safe.

senses.definition: To cause to make a sharp sound.
senses.example: to crack a whip

senses.definition: To tell (a joke).
senses.example: The performance was fine until he cracked that dead baby joke.

senses.definition: To circumvent software restrictions such as regional coding or time limits.
senses.example: That software license will expire tomorrow unless we can crack it.

senses.definition: To open a canned beverage, or any packaged drink or food.
senses.example: I'd love to crack open a beer.

senses.definition: To barely reach or attain (a measurement or extent).
senses.example: An underground band that never cracked the Hot 100

senses.definition: To have sex, especially penetrative sex (with).
senses.example: Did you hear about Josh cracking Stacy in the school hall?

senses.definition: To break down (a complex molecule), especially with the application of heat: to pyrolyse.
senses.example: Acetone is cracked to ketene and methane at 700°C.

senses.definition: A thin and usually jagged space opened in a previously solid material.
senses.example: A large crack had formed in the roadway.

senses.definition: A narrow opening.
senses.example: We managed to squeeze through a crack in the rock wall.

senses.definition: A sharply humorous comment; a wisecrack.
senses.example: I didn't appreciate that crack about my hairstyle.

senses.definition: Crack cocaine, a potent, relatively cheap, addictive variety of cocaine; often a rock, usually smoked through a crack pipe.
senses.example: crack head

senses.definition: Something pleasurable (good-tasting or appealing) and habit-forming.
senses.example: kitty crack

senses.definition: The sharp sound made when solid material breaks.
senses.example: The crack of the falling branch could be heard for miles.

senses.definition: Any sharp sound.
senses.example: The crack of the bat hitting the ball.

senses.definition: A sharp, resounding blow.
senses.example: He landed a crack to the jaw that dropped the attacker instantly.

senses.definition: An attempt at something.
senses.example: I'd like to take a crack at that game.

senses.definition: The vagina.
The space between the buttocks.
senses.example: Pull up your pants! Your crack is showing.

senses.definition: A program or procedure designed to circumvent restrictions or usage limits on software.
senses.example: Has anyone got a crack for DocumentWriter 3.0?

senses.definition: Extremely silly, absurd or off-the-wall ideas or prose.
senses.example: Her latest screenplay is pure crack, full of absurd ideas that nobody could follow.

senses.definition: The tone of voice when changed at puberty.
senses.example: At thirteen he hated the crack in his voice whenever he tried to sing.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) Breach of chastity.
Dry firewood.
(uncommon) A flaw, weakness, setback, or insecurity.
senses.example: Her interview answer revealed a crack in her confidence that the panel noticed.
senses.label: uncommon

senses.definition: An expanding circle of white water surrounding the site of a large explosion at shallow depth, marking the progress of the shock wave through the air above the water.A nuclear explosion in shallow water; the crack is clearly visible on the water's surface.
senses.example: The crack spread across the bay within seconds of the underwater blast.

senses.definition: (dated) The act of hitting on someone.
senses.example: Back in the 1950s, Ray made a crack at the girl by the jukebox.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Highly trained and competent.
senses.example: Even a crack team of investigators would have trouble solving this case.

senses.definition: Excellent, first-rate, superior, top-notch.
senses.example: She's a crack shot with that rifle.

core.definition: To break or split partly, leaving a line or gap without coming completely apart; to give way under strain.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with the short a of 'cat' and a clear k at the end. Do not add a vowel after the k; say it crisp, not 'crack-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; negative when it describes damage or breakdown, and positive in phrases like crack the code.
nuance.usage_note: The verb covers physical and figurative breaking: a cracked windshield, a cracked rib, or a person who cracks under pressure. Americans also say crack a window to open it slightly, and crack a joke to make a witty remark. In everyday talk, to crack the code means to solve a hard puzzle.

distinctions.note: Break means to separate into pieces; crack means a partial break or split with a line, though it may later break completely.
Chip removes a small piece from an edge, while crack is a line or split running through the material.
Fracture is the technical or medical word for a break in bone or material; crack is the everyday word.

examples.everyday: Be careful with that mug, the handle is starting to crack.
examples.professional: Our integration tests crack under heavy load, so we need to find where the connection pool is failing.
examples.analytical: Some arguments crack not because their conclusions are false but because a weak premise has been quietly assumed.

nuance.analogy: A crack in a sidewalk: the surface still looks whole, but a line of weakness runs through it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English crakken, related to Old English cracian, to make a sharp noise.
common_mistakes: Confusing crack with crash, which means a violent collision or fall rather than a split.
Using crack up to mean break; in American English crack up usually means to laugh hard.

crack.etymology: From Middle English *crakken*, *craken*, from Old English *cracian* (“to resound; to crack”), from **krakōn* (“to crack; to crackle; to shriek”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **gerh₂-* (“to resound; to cry hoarsely”).

senses.definition: Something created such as an invention or artwork.
senses.example: I think the manufacturer was so ashamed of its creation that it didn't put its name on it!

senses.definition: The act of creating something.
senses.example: The restructure resulted in the creation of a number of shared services.

senses.definition: All which exists.
senses.example: Let us pray to Christ, the King of all creation.

core.definition: The act of bringing something into existence, or something that has been made, such as an invention or artwork; in theology, God's bringing the universe into being.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the AY syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced 'shun', not 'shee-on'. Keep the initial r clear and avoid a separate long 'ee' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; in religious contexts it carries reverence and awe, and in art or cooking it praises original work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use creation for both the act of making and the finished thing, as in 'This dessert is my latest creation.' When capitalized, or in religious talk, it means the universe as made by God, and it is also central to debates about Creation versus evolution. Used casually it can sound a bit grand, so 'my latest thing' is more relaxed.

distinctions.note: An invention is a new device, process or method; creation is broader and can include art, food, ideas or the whole universe.
Making is the ordinary process of producing something; creation suggests something original, impressive or created from nothing in theology.

examples.everyday: Check out my latest creation, a chocolate cake with raspberries on top.
examples.professional: The new dashboard is my creation, so send any feedback to me directly.
examples.analytical: Karl Barth treats the doctrine of creation as the foundation for understanding God's covenant with humanity.

nuance.analogy: A creation is the finished cake, while creation is the whole act of baking it from raw ingredients.
nuance.etymology: From Latin creatio, from creare, to create, with a root sense of bringing forth.
common_mistakes: Saying kree-AY-shee-on; the final syllable is 'shun'.
Using creation for a living being; the right words are creature or creator.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew bara' (to create), used of God's creative work in Genesis 1:1, and Greek ktisis (creation, the created order) as in Romans 8:19-22, with the related verb ktizo in Colossians 1:16. Genesis 1:1 states that God created the heavens and the earth, which is the foundational statement of the doctrine. Romans 8:19-22 describes the created world as sharing in the hope of redemption, and Colossians 1:15-17 presents Christ as the firstborn over all creation through whom all things were made.

traditions.view: God creates all things out of nothing by his will and through the Word, and Orthodox theologians have generally held a broad, non-literal reading of the Genesis days while stressing that creation is a gift that reveals God.
The Church teaches that God creates all things from nothing, and it accepts that the human body may have developed over time, while affirming that God directly creates each human soul.

Young-earth creationists read Genesis as six literal days a few thousand years ago, old-earth creationists accept an ancient earth, and theistic evolutionists see evolution as God's method; Reformed, Lutheran, Baptist and other traditions hold a range of these views.

creation.etymology: Middle English *creacion*, from Old French *creacion*, from Latin *creātiō*.

senses.definition: A human.
senses.example: She's the most beautiful creature I've ever laid eyes on.

senses.definition: A living being; an animal, monster, or alien, often as distinct from a human being.
senses.example: insects and other creatures

senses.definition: A being subservient to or dependent upon another.
senses.example: The dog is a loyal creature who depends on its owner for food, shelter, and affection.

senses.definition: A result or product of something; a (figurative) creation.
senses.example: He's a creature of circumstance.

senses.definition: (rare) A thing or being that has been created; a creation.
senses.example: Theologians have long debated whether humans, as creatures of God, possess free will.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A living being, especially an animal, or sometimes a human, monster or imaginary being.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The final -ure is a reduced 'chur' sound, not 'chure', and the 'tch' is one clear sound as in 'church'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to affectionate for animals, but negative when used for monsters or to describe a person in a demeaning way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use creature for animals, especially in stories or affectionate talk, as in 'the little creatures in the pond,' and for monsters in movies. Calling a person a creature sounds odd or insulting depending on tone. The phrase 'poor creature' sounds sympathetic. In formal or biblical speech, creature can mean any created being.

distinctions.note: Animal is the general term, while creature is more vivid and can include imagined beings or, in old usage, people.
Beast often suggests a large, wild or threatening animal, while creature is neutral or affectionate.
Being is abstract and philosophical, while creature emphasizes a living thing that was made or depends on something else.

examples.everyday: Look at those little creatures in the tide pool.
examples.professional: The wildlife team tagged several creatures in the marsh so we can track their movement this summer.
examples.analytical: Aquinas distinguishes God as creator from every creature, since created things receive their being rather than possess it necessarily.

nuance.etymology: From Latin creatura, a created thing, from creare, to create.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it kree-AY-chur; the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Calling a person a creature in formal English, which can sound demeaning.
