In professional settings, say "animated GIF" or "short video clip" if you want to be formal. Someone might say "Send a GIF" or "Drop a GIF in the channel" in casual chat.

distinctions.note: An MP4 is a video format with sound and higher quality; a GIF usually has no sound and uses fewer colors.
A PNG is a still image format; a GIF can contain several frames and animate.

examples.everyday: My sister sent me a funny GIF of a cat falling off a couch.
examples.professional: Could you drop a quick GIF of the bug in the team channel so we can see what happens?
examples.analytical: The GIF format's limited palette and lossless frame encoding shape the kind of motion it can represent well.

nuance.analogy: Like a flipbook made of a few dozen pictures that loops forever.
nuance.etymology: Short for Graphics Interchange Format, the format introduced by CompuServe in 1987.
common_mistakes: Using GIF as a plural in the wrong place; say "GIFs" with an s.
Saying "gif" with a soft g as in "giant" in technical discussions, where the word is usually pronounced with a hard g.

conversation.text: He replied with a funny GIF of a dancing cat.
Send me that GIF; I love it.
Our group chat is basically just GIFs.

senses.definition: To utter, publish; to announce, proclaim, report.
To announce (a hymn) to be sung; to read out (the words) for the congregation to sing.
To send forth, emit; to cause to be sent forth.
To put forth, utter (prayers).
To issue; to distribute.
senses.example: Can you help me to give out the new books to the class, please?

senses.definition: To cease functioning in some way. To desist.
senses.example: So your old car finally gave out, did it?

senses.definition: To desist.
To desist through exhaustion of strength or patience.
To break down, get out of order, fail.
senses.example: So your old car finally gave out, did it?

senses.definition: To run short, come to an end.
To pretend or act as if something is true.
senses.example: I gave out that I was at home, but they didn't ask for an alibi.

senses.definition: To express oneself intensely emotionally, either by talking or in a musical performance.
senses.example: He's been giving out for hours.

senses.definition: To deem (a player) to be out.
senses.example: The umpire controversially gave him out.

core.definition: To distribute things, one by one, to a group of people; also, to run out or stop working.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OUT, with 'give' carrying a lighter secondary stress. Be careful with the diphthong in 'out', which is /aʊt/, not a short 'oo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it describes an everyday action or a failure without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'give out' when handing things to a group, such as flyers, candy, or assignments. It also means a supply or energy has run out, as in 'my patience gave out'. In the sense 'stop working', it is used for machines and bodies, like 'the engine gave out'. It is different from 'give up', which means to quit.

distinctions.note: Hand out emphasizes physically passing items to people, while give out is common for both distribution and for running out or failing.
Give up means to quit or surrender, while give out means to distribute or to run out of something.
Run out refers to a supply being used up, while give out can also mean a machine or body fails.

examples.everyday: The neighbors gave out candy to every kid who came to the door on Halloween.
examples.professional: Could you give out the agenda before the meeting starts so everyone can follow along?
examples.analytical: Scholars note that the grant committee gave out funds unevenly, favoring institutions that were already well connected.

nuance.analogy: Like a teacher passing out worksheets one by one until the stack runs out.
nuance.etymology: 'Give' from Old English giefan, and 'out' from Old English ut.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'give out' with 'give up', so that someone says 'I gave out smoking' when they mean quit.
Using 'give out' for emitting heat or light in casual speech, where 'give off' is more common.

senses.definition: Relating to, or exhibiting, glossolalia.

core.definition: Relating to glossolalia, which is speech in unknown or ecstatic language, especially in religious worship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, 'LAL', so don't say 'GLAH-suh-lal-ik'. The middle vowel is a reduced 'uh', and the final 'ic' is short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarly or religious settings; it can sound judgmental if used to mock a worship practice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'glossolalic' mostly in academic writing about religion, psychology, or church history. In church conversation, people more often say 'speaking in tongues' or 'praying in the Spirit'. Using the adjective in a friendly talk about someone's faith can sound clinical or dismissive, so be careful with tone.

distinctions.note: Speaking in tongues is the everyday phrase used by believers; glossolalic is a technical adjective used in study and description.
Xenoglossy means speaking a real foreign language one has never learned; glossolalia usually is not a recognizable language.

examples.everyday: My friend's church has a glossolalic prayer time, and people speak in tongues during worship.
examples.professional: When we teach the history of Pentecostalism, we should describe glossolalic practices without mocking them.
examples.analytical: Paul's treatment of glossolalic speech in 1 Corinthians distinguishes private prayer from public teaching in the assembly.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio playing a station you cannot understand: the sound is there and meaningful to some listeners, but it is not in the language you speak.
nuance.etymology: From Greek glōssa (tongue) and lalia (speech), via glossolalia.
common_mistakes: Using glossolalic for a real foreign language; the word refers to ecstatic speech, not a learned language.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'GLAH-suh-lal-ik'; the stress falls on LAL.
nuance.biblical_note: The key Greek phrase is glōssais lalein (to speak in tongues), where glōssa means tongue or language. Acts 2:4 describes the disciples at Pentecost beginning to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. First Corinthians 14:2 says that one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God, and 1 Corinthians 14:4 says such a speaker builds up himself. Paul in chapters 12 to 14 insists that tongues must be interpreted in the assembly so the church is edified.

traditions.view: Orthodox churches generally regard glossolalia as a gift of the Spirit that was given in the apostolic age, but they do not treat it as a required sign of baptism or holiness and discourage ecstatic practices outside ordered worship.

The Catholic Church recognizes tongues as a charism given by the Spirit, but Catholic teaching requires that it be discerned and ordered for the good of the church and that it is not the sign of full spiritual life.

Pentecostal and charismatic Protestants see tongues as a present gift and sometimes as evidence of Spirit baptism, while many Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican, and Baptist churches hold that such gifts ceased with the apostolic age or are rare and must be interpreted.

senses.definition: Despondent; moody; sullen.
senses.example: Ever since the layoffs, Dan has been quiet and glum at every team meeting.

core.definition: Feeling or looking sad, gloomy, or unhappy, often quietly and without energy, as after bad news.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short 'u' as in 'bum' or 'sun', not the long 'oo' of 'gloom'. End cleanly on the m with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative but mild. It describes a low, quiet mood rather than deep grief.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glum in everyday talk about a mood or face after a lost game, a rainy weekend, or bad news. It is neutral and descriptive, slightly literary in tone. In very casual speech people might say 'bummed' or 'down' instead, but glum is common in news, fiction, and general conversation.

distinctions.note: Sad is stronger and more general; glum describes a quieter, more sullen or resigned mood, often shown on the face.
Gloomy often describes dark weather or places, or a pessimistic outlook; glum describes a person's mood.
Moody suggests a changeable, unpredictable temper; glum describes steady low spirits.

examples.everyday: You look glum. Did the Yankees lose again?
examples.professional: The team went quiet and glum after the client rejected the demo.
examples.analytical: Some readers hear Ecclesiastes as a glum meditation on labor, yet its repeated call to enjoy simple gifts complicates that mood.

nuance.analogy: A glum mood is like a cloud sitting low over the day: not a storm, just a heaviness that won't lift.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; likely related to gloom and the older English verb glum, to frown.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long u like 'gloom' (GLOOM) instead of short u (GLUM).
Using glum as a noun, as in 'the glum,' instead of as an adjective.

glum.etymology: Probably from *glum* (“glum”), related to dialectal *glumm* (“gloomy, troubled, turbid”).

senses.definition: An excess, too much.
senses.example: a glut of the market

senses.definition: That which is swallowed.
senses.example: The heron struggled to swallow its glut, a frog nearly as big as its head.

senses.definition: Something that fills up an opening.
senses.example: A rag served as a glut in the hole, keeping the wind from whistling through the cabin.

senses.definition: A wooden wedge used in splitting blocks.
senses.example: The woodcutter drove a glut into the split log to widen the crack.

senses.definition: A piece of wood used to fill up behind cribbing or tubbing.
senses.example: Workers packed a wooden glut behind the cribbing to keep the mine shaft wall from shifting.

senses.definition: A bat, or small piece of brick, used to fill out a course.
senses.example: The mason cut a brick glut to fill the last gap in the course.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) A block used for a fulcrum.
The broad-nosed eel (Anguilla anguilla, syn. Anguilla latirostris), found in Europe, Asia, the West Indies, etc.
senses.example: Anglers on the river occasionally hooked a glut, the broad-nosed eel, before dawn.

senses.definition: An arched opening to the ashpit of a kiln.
senses.example: Before lighting the kiln, the potter cleared ash from the arched glut beneath the firebox.

senses.definition: To fill to capacity; to satisfy all demand or requirement; to sate.
senses.example: to glut one's appetite

senses.definition: To provide (a market) with so much of a product that the supply greatly exceeds the demand.
senses.example: Cheap imports began to glut the market, and local farmers could not sell their apples.

senses.definition: To eat gluttonously or to satiety.
senses.example: After the holiday feast, the twins glut themselves on pie until they could barely stand.

core.definition: An excess or oversupply of something, so that there is far more than is needed or wanted.

pronunciation.tip: It has one syllable with a short 'uh' vowel, like 'cut' and 'but.' Do not stretch the vowel into 'glaht' or 'gloot.'

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It implies too much of something, which can be wasteful, unhealthy, or bad for prices.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glut in business and news, as in 'a glut of housing' or 'a glut on the market.' In everyday talk people often say 'too much' or 'more than enough,' but glut sounds natural in economic discussions. Using it for food sounds more informal and slightly dramatic.

distinctions.note: Surplus is a neutral term for extra supply; glut suggests a larger, more problematic excess that pushes prices down.
Excess is a general word for too much; glut is more specific to supply, markets, or overabundance.

examples.everyday: There's a glut of zucchini in our garden this year, so I keep giving it away.
examples.professional: We have a glut of unused licenses, so finance wants us to cut the subscription before renewal.
examples.analytical: Economists argue that a glut of savings can depress interest rates even when investment opportunities are limited.

nuance.analogy: Like a river overflowing its banks: there is more water than the channel can carry, so it spreads everywhere.
nuance.etymology: From Old French gloutir, to swallow, from Latin glutire.
common_mistakes: Using glut as a verb with the wrong preposition, such as glut with instead of glut the market
Confusing glut with gluttony, which describes excessive eating as a vice

glut.etymology: Middle English *glotien//glotten*, probably Old French *gloter//glotir//glotoiier* [compare, ], Latin *gluttiō*.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see go,‎ past.
To elapse.
senses.example: That hour went past so quickly!

senses.definition: To surpass a boundary; to go by a limit.

core.definition: To move beyond a place, point or limit without stopping, or to exceed a boundary. Used for vehicles, people walking, and time passing.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are one syllable, and the stress falls on 'past,' so the particle 'go' is lighter. Keep the vowel in 'past' short and open, as in 'cat' with a t at the end, not a long 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes movement or time and carries no judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'go past' constantly for directions, such as 'It's the house just past the gas station.' For giving something to someone at the table, say 'pass' instead, since 'go past' sounds odd there. Time also 'goes past' in literary or reflective speech, though 'pass' is more common for time.

distinctions.note: 'Pass' is more common for moving by a point or handing things over, and it is the usual word for time. 'Go past' is more concrete and directional.
'Go by' is slightly more casual and often means going near something in passing, as in 'We went by the bank on the way home.'

collocations: the bus goes past my house

examples.everyday: Turn left at the gas station, and you'll go past the library before you get to my house.
examples.professional: We can't let the project budget go past the approved limit without a sign-off from finance.
examples.analytical: An argument that goes past its premises has to earn each new conclusion instead of inheriting it from the start.

nuance.analogy: Like a car on a highway that drives past an exit: it keeps moving and does not stop at that point.
nuance.etymology: 'Go' comes from Old English 'gān'; 'past' is from an earlier form of 'pass.'
common_mistakes: Using 'go past' to mean 'pass' when handing something over, as in 'Go past me the salt' instead of 'Pass me the salt.'
Adding 'to' before 'past' as in 'go to past the store.'

senses.definition: An intermediary or middleman.
senses.example: She's the go-between for engineering and manufacturing, so you'll have to ask her if you need to coordinate between the groups.

senses.definition: A shogi piece, used in chu shogi and larger shogi variants, that can move one step straight forward or straight backwards.
senses.example: In chu shogi, the go-between piece moves one step straight forward or backward.

core.definition: A person who carries messages or negotiates between two people or groups who do not communicate directly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second word, 'between,' on its second syllable, 'TWEEN.' The first syllable of 'between' is a reduced 'bih,' so don't pronounce it as 'bee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest secrecy or manipulation when the go-between has hidden motives.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'go-between' for people who pass messages between family members, coworkers, or business partners. It is less formal than 'intermediary' and more personal than 'mediator.' Stories about a go-between often involve tension, so people may respond with 'Oh, so you were the messenger?'

distinctions.note: 'Intermediary' is more formal and is used in diplomacy, law, or finance, while 'go-between' is everyday and personal.
A mediator is formally appointed to help parties reach agreement, while a go-between may only pass messages without guiding the outcome.

collocations: a go-between for the two families

examples.everyday: My sister acted as a go-between when Mom and Dad weren't speaking.
examples.professional: As the go-between for the vendor and our finance team, Maria keeps both sides informed.
examples.analytical: The broker functions as a go-between whose advantage depends on the opacity of the market.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge that carries traffic but does not own either side of the river.
nuance.etymology: A compound of 'go' and 'between,' describing one who moves between two parties.
common_mistakes: Writing 'gobetween' as one word or dropping the hyphen; the standard form is 'go-between.'
Using 'go between' as a noun; 'go between' is a verb phrase, so say 'act as a go-between' for the noun.

senses.definition: A peanut.
A foolish, simple, or amusingly silly person.
senses.example: Don't be such a goober, Eddie, you'll never get the girl that way.

senses.definition: A quantity of sputum.
senses.example: The nurse wrote down the color of the goober he coughed up that morning.

senses.definition: A Georgian or North Carolinian, particularly one from the pine forests of the Sandhills region.
senses.example: My cousin from the Sandhills calls himself a goober, and he's proud of it.

senses.definition: To drool or dribble.
senses.example: The sleepy toddler goobered on his pillow while his grandmother read the bedtime story.

senses.definition: To drip or slather; to apply a gooey substance to a surface.
senses.example: She goobered peanut butter all over the toast before handing it to her brother.

core.definition: A peanut, a regional Southern American word. Also a playful term for a silly, awkward person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GOO. The final syllable is the American r-colored schwa, so it sounds like 'ber' and not 'bar'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the peanut sense; playful, often affectionate, for a silly person, though it can sting in an insult.
nuance.usage_note: In the American South, goober is the everyday word for a peanut, especially in rural areas, at fairs or at roadside stands. Most Americans elsewhere say peanut and may not know the word. Used for a person, it is casual and can be affectionate or mildly teasing, and it is often used for Georgians or North Carolinians. A natural reply to 'Want some goobers?' is 'Sure, thanks!'

distinctions.note: Peanut is the standard American word everywhere; goober is a Southern and folksy alternative.
Goofball clearly means a silly, oddball person; goober is softer and can be affectionate.

examples.everyday: Grab me a bag of goobers from the gas station, would you?
examples.professional: The agricultural report uses peanut throughout, although growers in the South often say goober informally.
examples.analytical: The survival of goober in Southern speech preserves an African origin for a crop that reached the American South through the slave trade.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a soda pop in Ohio: a local name for a familiar thing.
nuance.etymology: Probably from a Bantu word such as Kikongo nguba, meaning peanut.
common_mistakes: Assuming goober always means a silly person; in much of the South it simply means a peanut.
Pronouncing the second syllable as bar; it is a light, reduced r-colored vowel.

senses.definition: Farewell; a formula used to another person or persons when the speaker, writer, or person addressed is departing.
senses.example: Goodbye, and drive safely on the way home tonight.

senses.definition: An utterance of goodbye, the wishing of farewell to someone.
senses.example: They made their good-byes.

senses.definition: To say goodbye; to wish somebody farewell on parting.
senses.example: She goodbyes every guest at the door with a hug and a tiny wave.

core.definition: A word said when leaving or ending a conversation, visit, or phone call; a polite farewell.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on BYE, and good is quick and light. In casual speech the d is often barely heard, so it sounds like 'guh-BYE.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to polite. It can sound final or sad, especially when someone is leaving for a long time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say goodbye at the end of most conversations, visits, and business calls, although on the phone or in texts they often say bye or see you. Goodbye can sound final, so it is less common when you expect to talk again soon. A natural reply is simply goodbye, bye, see you, or take care.

distinctions.note: Bye is casual and very common on phone calls and in texts; goodbye is fuller and more polite.
See you implies you will meet again soon; goodbye does not promise a future meeting.
Farewell is formal, literary, or used for a long departure; goodbye is everyday English.

examples.everyday: Thanks for the ride. Goodbye, and text me when you get home safely.
examples.professional: Thanks, everyone, for joining. Goodbye, and I'll see you at next week's standup.
examples.analytical: Commentators often read Jesus' farewell discourse in John as more than a goodbye, since it also promises his continued presence.

nuance.analogy: Like closing a door gently behind you: you leave, but with a sign of respect and care.
nuance.etymology: Contraction of 'God be with ye,' a blessing said at parting.
common_mistakes: Writing good-bye or goodby, which are old or nonstandard forms; modern American writing uses goodbye.
Using goodbye as a casual greeting or to start a conversation.
Confusing it with bye-bye, which is informal and often used for children.

synonyms: see you in the funny papers
goodbye.etymology: From earlier *goodby*, *Godby*, *Godby'e*, *Godbwye*, *God b'w'y*, *God bwy yee*, *God buy you*, *God be wi' you*, each a progressively shorter contraction of or *God be with you*.

core.definition: The third book of the New Testament, a Gospel traditionally ascribed to Luke, known for its emphasis on mercy, the poor and prayer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GAH and LOOK, and 'of' reduces to 'uv'. Luke rhymes with 'book', so the vowel is short, not the long 'oo' of 'loose'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a reference; reverent in religious use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the Gospel of Luke' in formal settings and just 'Luke' in Bible study, as in 'We're in Luke this month.' Pastors often mention its birth stories and parables. The capital G marks the book, while lowercase gospel means the good news.

distinctions.note: Acts was written by the same author as Luke's Gospel and continues the story into the early church.
John has a distinct theology and structure; Luke is more narrative and historical in tone.
Mark is brief and fast-paced, while Luke adds birth narratives and a formal preface.

collocations: the nativity story in the Gospel of Luke
the parables in the Gospel of Luke
the preface to the Gospel of Luke
a passage from the Gospel of Luke

examples.everyday: My daughter is memorizing the Christmas story from the Gospel of Luke for the church pageant.
examples.professional: For the workshop on mercy, I'm using the parables in the Gospel of Luke because they give the clearest examples.
examples.analytical: The preface to the Gospel of Luke claims a careful investigation of earlier accounts, and scholars read that claim as a key to its method.

nuance.analogy: Like a careful historian who interviews witnesses and arranges the story in order, Luke presents Jesus's life as a sequenced account.
nuance.etymology: From Old English godspel, 'good news,' a translation of Greek euangelion.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing Luke with a long 'oo' like 'loose'; it rhymes with 'book'.
Writing 'Gospel of Saint Luke' in everyday speech; Americans usually say 'the Gospel of Luke' or just 'Luke'.
Assuming Luke was an eyewitness to Jesus; the text does not claim that, and tradition names him as a companion of Paul.
nuance.biblical_note: Luke 1:1-4 is the author's preface to Theophilus, explaining that he has investigated the sources carefully. Luke 4:18-19 has Jesus read from Isaiah in the synagogue, announcing good news to the poor. Luke 15 contains the parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin and the prodigal son, all about God's search for the lost. The root word is Greek euangelion, 'good news.'

senses.definition: Someone who likes to talk about other people's private or personal business.
senses.example: Be careful what you say to him: he’s a bit of a gossip.

senses.definition: Idle talk about someone’s private or personal matters, especially about someone not present.
senses.example: According to the latest gossip, their relationship is on the rocks.

senses.definition: A genre in contemporary media, usually focused on the personal affairs of celebrities.
senses.example: a gossip columnist

senses.definition: Communication done using a gossip protocol.
senses.example: The cluster nodes spread membership updates through gossip, so every server eventually learns about failures.

senses.definition: Idle conversation in general.
senses.example: Our Saturday morning gossip over pancakes drifted from baseball to the weather.

senses.definition: Title used with the name of one's child's godparent or of a friend.
senses.example: Gossip Mary, can you watch the baby on Thursday?

senses.definition: (historical) A sponsor; a godfather or godmother; the godparent of one's child or godchild, or the parent of one's godchild.
senses.example: In the sixteenth century, a child's gossip was expected to vouch for its Christian upbringing.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To talk about someone else's private or personal business, especially in a manner that spreads the information.
senses.example: Neighbors gossip about the Morrisons' divorce whenever they see the moving truck.

senses.definition: To talk idly.
senses.example: On the porch, we gossiped for hours about nothing in particular.

senses.definition: To communicate using a gossip protocol.
senses.example: Each node will gossip its routing table to a few random peers every second.

core.definition: Idle talk about other people's private or personal affairs, often unkind or spread without their knowledge.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the second syllable a short, quick 'sip' with a reduced vowel. Do not stretch the 'o' into a long 'oh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gossip' for talk about other people's private lives, usually among friends, coworkers or neighbors. It is informal, and calling someone a gossip is an insult. Informal speakers often say 'Did you hear the latest dish?' or 'Spill the tea', but 'gossip' is the neutral word. A natural reply to a juicy story is 'No way! Tell me more.'

distinctions.note: A rumor is an unverified claim spread about a situation, while gossip is focused on personal details about a particular person.
A chat is a friendly conversation about anything, while gossip specifically involves talking about others' private matters.

examples.everyday: Don't tell Maria that, she loves to spread gossip about the neighbors.
examples.professional: Management reminded the team that office gossip about performance reviews undermines trust.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have argued that gossip plays a social role by enforcing shared norms, although it can also cause harm.

nuance.analogy: Gossip is like a rumor mill that turns private details into a story passed hand to hand.
nuance.etymology: From Old English godsibb, meaning 'godparent', which later came to mean a close friend and then a chatty person.
common_mistakes: Using 'gossip' as a countable noun without an article, as in 'He told me a gossip' instead of 'He told me some gossip'.
Confusing 'gossip' with 'rumor' and using them interchangeably in formal writing.

gossip.etymology: From Middle English *gossib*, *godsib* (“a close friend or relation, a confidant; a godparent”), from Old English *godsibb* (“godparent, sponsor”), equivalent to *god-* + *sib*.

conversation.text: Did you hear the latest gossip about the new manager?
My aunts love to gossip at family dinners.
Don't tell Jake anything. He's such a gossip.

senses.definition: A rating.
senses.example: This fine-grade coin from 1837 is worth a good amount.

senses.definition: A degree or level of something; a position within a scale; a degree of quality.
senses.example: The restaurant served beef of a much higher grade than the one across town.

senses.definition: Degree (any of the three stages (positive, comparative, superlative) in the comparison of an adjective or an adverb).
senses.example: Students learned that the superlative grade of an adjective often ends in -est.

senses.definition: A slope (up or down) of a roadway or other passage.
senses.example: The grade of this hill is more than 5 percent.

senses.definition: A student of a particular grade (used with the grade level).
senses.example: The grade fives are on a field trip.

senses.definition: An area that has been flattened by a grader (construction machine).
senses.example: The grader left a smooth grade across the lot before the concrete trucks arrived.

senses.definition: The level of the ground.
senses.example: This material absorbs moisture and is probably not a good choice for use below grade.

senses.definition: A gradian.
senses.example: The survey instrument reported the slope as 25 grades rather than in degrees.

senses.definition: In a linear system of divisors on an n-dimensional variety, the number of free intersection points of n generic divisors.
senses.example: The grade of that linear system equals the count of intersection points of three generic divisors.

senses.definition: A harsh scraping or cutting; a grating.
senses.example: The gate hinge let out a grade that set my teeth on edge.

senses.definition: A taxon united by a level of morphological or physiological complexity that is not a clade.
senses.example: Some biologists argue that reptiles form a grade rather than a true clade.

senses.definition: The degree of malignity of a tumor expressed on a scale.
senses.example: The pathologist reported that the tumor was a high grade, requiring immediate treatment.

senses.definition: To assign scores to the components of an academic test, or to overall academic performance.
senses.example: The professor will grade the exams over the weekend and post results on Monday.

senses.definition: To organize in grades.
senses.example: a graded reader

senses.definition: To flatten, level, or smooth a large surface, especially with a grader.
senses.example: to grade land before building on it

senses.definition: To remove or trim part of a seam allowance from a finished seam so as to reduce bulk and make the finished piece more even when turned right side out.
senses.example: Before turning the collar, grade the seam allowance so the edges lie flat.

senses.definition: To increase or decrease the dimensions of a garment pattern from the initial base size in such a way that the overall proportions of the silhouette are maintained across all sizes.
senses.example: The designer had to grade the bodice pattern up to every size while keeping the proportions.

senses.definition: To apply classifying labels to data (typically by a manual rather than automatic process).
senses.example: Brain scans were graded on a five-point scale of atrophy.

senses.definition: To describe, modify or inflect so as to classify as to degree.
senses.example: Linguists grade these adjectives by intensity, placing warm below hot on the scale.

senses.definition: To pass imperceptibly from one grade into another.
senses.example: Twilight seems to grade into night so gradually that nobody notices the exact moment.

senses.definition: (dated) To pass from one school grade into the next.
senses.example: I graded out of grade two and three and arrived in Miss Hanson's room.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A mark or rating that shows how well a student or a piece of work performed, or a level of quality.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long a sound, and the final d is clear. Do not add a vowel after the d, as in grade-uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a rating or level, and it can be positive or negative depending on the actual score.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use grade constantly for school marks, such as getting a good grade on a test, and for levels of quality, such as grade A eggs. Students also say grade for a school year, as in fifth grade. In casual speech, a good grade is a high mark, while a bad grade is a low one.

distinctions.note: A score is the number of points earned, while a grade is the letter or category assigned based on the score.
Level describes a position on a scale in general, while grade often suggests a standard rating or classification, as in grade A or grade school.

examples.everyday: My son brought home a good grade on his science test, so we celebrated at dinner.
examples.professional: The vendor's product met the highest quality grade in our internal review.
examples.analytical: A grade in this sense is a conventional measure, not a direct record of what a student has understood.

nuance.analogy: Like a thermometer reading, which gives a number that places something on a scale.
nuance.etymology: From Latin gradus, step, degree, through French grade, step or rank.
common_mistakes: Saying I have a grade in the school sense in the wrong way; say I got a grade or I got a good grade.
Pronouncing it as gray-duh; it is one syllable, grayd.

grade.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *grade* (“a grade, degree”), from Latin *gradus* (“a step, pace, degree”), from Proto-Italic **graðus*, from Proto-Indo-European **gʰradʰ-*, **gʰredʰ-* (“to walk, go”).

senses.definition: The belief that some phenomenon occurs gradually over a long period of time.
senses.example: Geologists still debate whether gradualism or catastrophe better explains the canyon's formation.

senses.definition: The belief that change ought to be brought about in small, discrete increments rather than in abrupt strokes such as revolutions or uprisings.
senses.example: Her gradualism frustrated activists who wanted immediate, sweeping change to the city's housing laws.

senses.definition: The belief that evolution proceeds at a steady pace, without the sudden development of new species or biological features from one generation to the next.
senses.example: Textbooks once presented gradualism as the only path of evolution, but punctuated equilibrium challenged that view.

core.definition: The belief that change, whether in society, nature, or science, happens slowly through small steps rather than through sudden, dramatic events.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on GRAD, and -ism is an unstressed ending ending in a schwa. Many learners pronounce the middle syllable as 'way' rather than a reduced 'wuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in reform and science contexts, and negative when critics use it to suggest excessive delay.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gradualism' mainly in political, historical, scientific, and academic discussion, not in casual conversation. In debates, it can be a compliment for careful reform or a criticism of moving too slowly. Use 'gradualist' for a person who holds this view.

distinctions.note: Gradualism stresses a slow, continuous process, while incrementalism in policy stresses small, tested steps that can be adjusted as results come in.
Catastrophism holds that sudden events drive major change, the opposite view from gradualism in geology and biology.

examples.everyday: He believes in gradualism, so he cut his coffee intake by one cup a week instead of quitting overnight.
examples.professional: The team's gradualism on the rewrite meant we kept the old system running for six months while we migrated users.
examples.analytical: Lyell's gradualism held that the earth's features are shaped by slow, continuous processes still observable today, rather than by sudden catastrophes.

nuance.analogy: Gradualism is like erosion: small, steady forces reshape the landscape over long periods.
nuance.etymology: From gradual and the suffix -ism, from Latin gradus, step.
common_mistakes: Confusing gradualism, the belief, with gradualist, the person who holds it.
Using gradualism for the simple fact of slowness; it means a belief or theory about change.

senses.definition: One who believes in gradualism.

core.definition: A person who believes that social, political or personal change should happen slowly, step by step, rather than through sudden or radical action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle 'du' is quick, closer to 'joo' than 'doo'. Don't add an extra 'w' or 'uh' sound between 'gradu' and 'al'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. Supporters of change may see a gradualist as sensible and patient, while critics may see one as timid or as a delayer of needed reform.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in discussions of politics, history, social reform, or philosophy, such as debates over abolition, civil rights, or climate policy. It is rarely used in casual talk. Saying you are 'a gradualist' signals a stance on how change should happen, not just that you move slowly.

distinctions.note: Both favor small steps, but incrementalist is more common in policy and technology talk and suggests building on each small improvement, while gradualist is used more in historical and political debates about how fundamental change should come.
A reformer wants to change a system, often in a major way; a gradualist agrees with reform in principle but insists it proceed slowly.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a gradualist when it comes to changing his diet, so he cut out one sugary drink a week instead of quitting all at once.
examples.professional: Our product lead is a gradualist, so she wants to roll the new pricing out to one region before we change it nationwide.
examples.analytical: Burke's position makes him a gradualist in the strict sense, since he holds that institutions survive only when they change through slow, accumulated adjustment rather than through sudden rupture.

nuance.analogy: A gradualist is like a hiker who follows switchbacks up a mountain instead of climbing straight up a cliff: slower, but far less likely to fall.
nuance.etymology: From gradual, from Medieval Latin gradualis, from Latin gradus 'step', plus the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Using gradualist to mean simply slow or lazy; it describes a belief about how change should happen, not a personal pace.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables as 'GRAD-yoo-wuh-list' with an extra 'w' sound.

senses.definition: The state of being guiltless; innocence.

core.definition: The state of not being responsible for wrongdoing; innocence and freedom from blame.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GILT. The -less and -ness endings reduce to short schwa sounds, so do not add extra syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it affirms that a person did not do wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use guiltlessness in formal writing, moral argument, religious discussion, and literary prose. Everyday speakers say innocent or not guilty instead. The word works in an essay or sermon but sounds stiff in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Innocence can be legal, moral, or childlike, while guiltlessness specifically means freedom from guilt for a particular wrong.
Guilelessness means sincerity without deceit, while guiltlessness means not being responsible for wrongdoing.
Blamelessness stresses that no one can fairly blame you, while guiltlessness focuses on the absence of guilt itself.

examples.everyday: After the cookies vanished, Tom insisted on his guiltlessness, though the crumbs said otherwise.
examples.professional: The audit confirmed the team's guiltlessness in the billing error, so no one was disciplined.
examples.analytical: Augustine distinguishes an outward innocence from the inward guiltlessness that the heart truly possesses before God.

nuance.analogy: Like a clean slate that has nothing written on it that could be held against you.
nuance.etymology: From guiltless, from guilt plus the suffix -less, with -ness added to make a noun.
common_mistakes: Confusing guiltlessness with guilelessness; guiltlessness means not guilty, guilelessness means sincere.
Using it in casual speech where innocent or not guilty sounds more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word naqi (נָקִי) means innocent, clean, or free from guilt. Exodus 20:7 in the RSV says the LORD will not hold guiltless anyone who takes his name in vain. Psalm 51:14 asks God to deliver the psalmist from bloodguiltiness, showing that guilt needs to be removed by God.

senses.definition: A hairstyle.
A haircut.
senses.example: She spent two hours at the salon getting a new hairdo for her sister's wedding.

core.definition: A hairstyle, especially one that has been carefully arranged or styled for a special occasion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HAIR and pronounce 'do' as one syllable, like 'do' in 'do it', not two syllables. The vowel is a long oo.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Complimenting someone's hairdo is a friendly, common gesture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hairdo informally, often when praising or commenting on a new style: 'I love your new hairdo!' It sounds a bit more casual than hairstyle and suggests effort in styling, such as for a wedding or a big event. For a simple cut, say haircut.

distinctions.note: A haircut is the cutting itself, while a hairdo is the styled result that people see.
Hairstyle is the more general and neutral term, while hairdo is more informal and often implies careful arranging.

examples.everyday: Wow, I love your new hairdo! Did you go to the salon?
examples.professional: The salon's marketing team wants the hairdos in the spring photos to match the new product line.
examples.analytical: The hairdo, with its tight curls and structured bangs, signaled respectability in the portraits of that period.

nuance.analogy: A hairdo is like the facade of a building: the first thing people see, shaped with deliberate effort.
nuance.etymology: Compound of hair and do, in the sense of arranging or fixing.
common_mistakes: Using hairdo for a simple trim; the word usually refers to styled hair.
Pronouncing hairdo with two syllables at the end, like 'HAIR-doo-ee'.

senses.definition: Having a lot of body hair.
senses.example: a hairy man

senses.definition: Having a lot of fur.
senses.example: hairy mammoth

senses.definition: Having hair growing from it.
senses.example: hairy chest; hairy back

senses.definition: Seeming as if hair-covered or as if consisting of hair.
senses.example: hairy cell leukemia

senses.definition: Difficult, complex, intricate, or intimidating.
senses.example: It’s a hairy problem, and will probably take several weeks to sort out.

senses.definition: Causing anxiety or fright; terrifying, scary.
senses.example: The final mile of the mountain descent was hairy, with loose gravel and steep drops.

senses.definition: (uncommon) Long-haired.
senses.example: yelling about dirty, hairy hippies
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: Covered with a lot of hair or fur.

pronunciation.tip: Two syllables, stress on the first, with the 'air' vowel and a rhotic R. Do not say 'HAY-ree'; the final y is a short ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing animals or people; informal slang for 'scary' or 'dangerous' ('a hairy situation'), which is often humorous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'a hairy dog' or 'a hairy chest' in neutral description, and in casual speech 'hairy' can mean a risky or messy situation. Calling a person hairy about their body can sound rude, so use it with care. The slang sense is common among friends.

distinctions.note: Furry suggests soft, thick fur on an animal or toy, while hairy is broader and can describe human body hair.
Shaggy means having long, untidy hair or fur, often with a messy look; hairy is more neutral.

examples.everyday: Our new puppy is so hairy that we vacuum the couch every day.
examples.professional: The hairy-looking lab sample turned out to be a fiber from the carpet, not a biological contaminant.
examples.analytical: In Genesis, Esau's hairy body is part of the story that lets Jacob deceive their father Isaac.

nuance.analogy: Like a sweater made of thick wool that covers everything, hairy describes a body or surface completely covered in hair.
nuance.etymology: From 'hair' (Old English hær) with the suffix '-y' meaning 'full of' or 'covered with'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'hairy' with two syllables in the wrong place, as 'HAIR-ee' is correct.
Using 'hairy' as an insult about a person's body in polite company.
nuance.biblical_note: Genesis 27:11 has Jacob point out to his mother Rebekah that Esau his brother is a hairy man, which is how Jacob could pass as Esau when deceiving his blind father Isaac. Genesis 27:23 says Isaac did not recognize Jacob because his hands were hairy like Esau's. Genesis 25:25 describes Esau at birth as red and hairy all over, like a garment.

senses.definition: The tragic flaw of the protagonist in a literary tragedy.
senses.example: Creon's main hamartia was his excessive pride.

senses.definition: Sin.
senses.example: In the sermon, the pastor described pride as the root hamartia that leads every person astray.

senses.definition: A focal malformation consisting of disorganized arrangement of tissue types.
senses.example: The pathologist noted a focal hamartia in the lung tissue during the biopsy review.

core.definition: In literary tragedy, the tragic flaw or error in a hero's character that leads to his downfall; in theology, sin.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'TEE,' the third syllable, with a secondary stress on 'HAM.' The 'r' is pronounced clearly, and the final vowel is a soft 'uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in literary criticism. In theological use it has a serious, negative tone meaning sin.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hamartia' mostly in literature classes and in writing about Aristotle's Poetics. In everyday speech they would say 'fatal flaw' or 'tragic flaw' instead. In theology, the Greek word is used when discussing the New Testament meaning of sin as missing the mark.

distinctions.note: Tragic flaw is the everyday English phrase for the same literary idea; hamartia is the technical Greek term, used mainly in classical criticism.
Sin is the general term in English for moral wrong; hamartia in the literary sense is an error that leads to tragedy, not necessarily a moral failing.

examples.everyday: In my book club we argued about whether Macbeth's ambition is his tragic flaw, which is what Aristotle would call hamartia.
examples.professional: In the English seminar, the instructor asked us to identify the hamartia in each protagonist before writing the essay.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's hamartia is best understood not as a moral vice but as an error of judgment that the audience can recognize as human, which is what makes the fall tragic.

nuance.analogy: Hamartia is like a crack in a strong vase: the vase may be beautiful, but the flaw is what eventually breaks it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hamartia, missing the mark or error, from hamartanein, to miss the mark.
common_mistakes: Using it as a general word for any mistake; in literature it means a tragic error or flaw.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable instead of 'TEE.'
Confusing it with 'hamartoma,' a medical term for a benign tumor-like growth.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament the Greek word hamartia, meaning missing the mark, is the common word for sin. Romans 3:23 of the RSV says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. Romans 6:23 says the wages of sin is death, and John 8:34 says that everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin. The word thus moves from a literary idea of tragic error to a theological idea of sin as a power that enslaves.

hamartia.etymology: From Ancient Greek *ἁμαρτία* (“tragic failure, sinful nature”), from the verb *ἁμαρτάνω* (“to miss the mark”).

senses.definition: A small settlement or a group of houses, often defined as a settlement smaller than a village or town with usually under two hundred people.
senses.example: After the highway bypassed it, the hamlet shrank to a church, a store, and a few farms.

senses.definition: An unincorporated community of whatever size, lacking its own municipal government, but with defined boundaries.
senses.example: The hamlet has no mayor or town council, so the county handles its roads.

senses.definition: An unincorporated community within an incorporated town. There are also incorporated villages within towns.
senses.example: The hamlet sits within the town limits, though it has no separate government of its own.

senses.definition: Any of the fish of the genus Hypoplectrus in the family Serranidae.
senses.example: The snorkel guide pointed out a blue hamlet hiding beneath the coral ledge.

core.definition: A very small community, smaller than a village, with few residents and usually no separate local government of its own.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like HAM-lit, not HAM-let with a full e. The l at the end is often syllabic, so you do not need an extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a place's size and character without judgment, though it can suggest a quiet, rural setting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hamlet mostly for tiny rural places, especially in New York and other northeastern states, where official names like hamlet and village have legal meanings. A person from a small town would more often say small town or just the name of the place. In everyday talk, a hamlet is simply a very small place with a few houses, a store, and maybe a church.

distinctions.note: A village is usually larger and may have its own local government, while a hamlet is smaller and often has no separate government.
A town is a larger municipal unit with more residents and services, whereas a hamlet is much smaller and often has no incorporated status.

collocations: a hamlet in upstate New York

examples.everyday: We stopped for gas in a little hamlet about ten minutes outside town.
examples.professional: The county planning office lists that area as a hamlet, so it does not have its own zoning board.
examples.analytical: The word hamlet carries an image of a small, bounded community whose identity depends on being distinct from larger centers of power.

nuance.analogy: A hamlet is like a single page of a town's story, a short passage that is complete but has no chapters of its own.
nuance.etymology: From Old French hamelet, a diminutive of hamel, meaning small village.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'let' vowel instead of a reduced schwa.
Confusing hamlet with the name of Shakespeare's play; the American pronunciation of the play's title is the same, but the word alone means a small place.

hamlet.etymology: From Middle English *hamlet*, *hamelet*, a borrowing from Old French *hamelet*, diminutive of Old French *hamel*, in turn diminutive of Old French *ham*, of origin, from **haim*, ultimately from Proto-Germanic **haimaz* (whence *home*).

senses.definition: Forceful, excessive, draconian, or abusive.
senses.example: The hard handed manager fired anyone who questioned his orders, creating a climate of fear.

senses.definition: Working-class; having hands hardened from labor.
senses.example: His hard handed father spent forty years on the docks, and his palms showed it.

core.definition: Harsh, forceful or oppressive in the way someone uses power or authority over others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HAN in 'handed'. The final '-ed' is pronounced 'id' in this adjective, and Americans often write it as one hyphenated word, hard-handed.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests excessive force, lack of mercy or abuse of power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans write this as hard-handed, with a hyphen. It is used for governments, police, managers, parents and landlords who rule harshly. It describes a style rather than a single act, and it is common in news and workplace discussion.

distinctions.note: Heavy-handed often means clumsy, overbearing or tactless, while hard-handed stresses harshness and severity.
Harsh is a broader word for anything severe or unpleasant. Hard-handed specifically describes a person or method of exercising power.
Draconian describes extremely severe laws or rules. Hard-handed describes the person or style of enforcement.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says the landlord is pretty hard-handed about late rent.
examples.professional: The new manager's hard-handed approach drove several good engineers to leave the team.
examples.analytical: Critics argued that the regime's hard-handed suppression of dissent undermined its legitimacy.

nuance.analogy: A hard-handed ruler is like a coach who uses fear rather than encouragement to get results.
nuance.etymology: From hard and hand, with the adjective suffix -ed.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two unhyphenated words in formal writing.
Pronouncing the final '-ed' as a separate syllable with a full 'ed' sound.

senses.definition: To nag about; to complain incessantly or persistently request; to continue to bring up as a point of contention.

core.definition: To keep talking about the same complaint, problem, or topic in a tiresome, repetitive way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the particle 'on,' so the verb 'harp' is lighter. Link the two words smoothly, so it sounds like 'hahr-PAHN' with a clear r at the start of 'harp.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes someone who keeps repeating a point in a way that annoys others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use harp on in everyday talk about someone who keeps repeating a complaint, such as 'Dad keeps harping on the thermostat.' It is informal but common, and it can be used at work when someone repeats an issue too often. A natural reply is 'Okay, I hear you' or 'I know, let's move on.' Do not use it as a polite way to ask a question.

distinctions.note: Nag means to repeatedly urge someone to do something, and it is directed at a person, while harp on usually refers to repeating a topic or complaint.
Dwell on means to think or talk at length about something, often painful, and can be neutral; harp on is more clearly annoying to others.

examples.everyday: Dad keeps harping on the thermostat, so I just turned it down and let him talk.
examples.professional: I don't want to harp on the deadline, but we are two weeks behind and need a plan.
examples.analytical: The essay harps on the same objection without ever answering the reply that the author has already given.

nuance.analogy: Harping on a point is like a song with one repeated line that keeps coming back until everyone wants a new tune.
nuance.etymology: The verb harp comes from Old English hearpe, the instrument; the figurative sense comes from the image of playing the same tune over and over.
common_mistakes: Saying 'harp about' without 'on'; 'harp on' is the standard phrasal verb, and 'harp on about' is informal British-leaning usage that Americans may find odd.
Confusing harp on with 'harp' the musical instrument; the phrasal verb is about repetition, not music.

senses.definition: Conveying in demeanour the assumption of superiority; disdainful, supercilious.

core.definition: Acting or looking as if you think you are better than others and they are beneath you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final vowel a clear 'ee'. Do not add a 'gh' sound; the 'gh' is silent, and the vowel is the 'aw' of 'caught'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests disdain and an unpleasant superiority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'haughty' mainly in descriptions of people's looks, voices or behavior, often in books, reviews or news writing. In everyday speech, 'snobby' or 'stuck-up' is more common. It is not rude to use, but it sounds more formal than most casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Proud can be positive, meaning pleased with an accomplishment, while haughty is always negative and implies looking down on others.
Arrogant is more general and common, while haughty specifically describes a cold, lofty manner of disdain.

examples.everyday: The hostess gave us a haughty look and said the wait would be an hour, even though the place was half empty.
examples.professional: The vendor's haughty replies in the email thread made the whole project team want to switch suppliers.
examples.analytical: Nietzsche often portrays the haughty aristocrat as someone who creates values for himself rather than seeking approval from others.

nuance.analogy: A haughty person is like someone standing on a balcony, looking down at a crowd as if they were not quite worth noticing.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English haute, from Old French haut, meaning high, from Latin altus.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a 'ow' sound as in 'how', which changes the word's sound.
Using 'haughty' to mean simply proud or confident in a positive sense.

senses.definition: However; despite what one has just stated.
senses.example: The plan sounds risky; having said that, it might still work.

core.definition: Even so; nevertheless, after stating something that qualifies or limits what was just said.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'said,' which rhymes with 'red,' not 'sayed.' 'That' is often reduced to a weak 'thuht' in fast speech, and the 'th' is voiced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a polite way to introduce a qualification or a counterpoint without sounding harsh.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in conversation, meetings, and writing to soften a point that follows praise or agreement. It is polite and common in both spoken and written English. It usually comes at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma, and often after a compliment. Natural replies include 'True, but' or 'Fair enough,' followed by the point.

distinctions.note: 'However' is more formal and works in writing, while 'having said that' is more conversational and marks a shift in tone.
'Nevertheless' is formal and stresses that something happened despite difficulties, whereas 'having said that' is looser and more spoken.
'That said' is a shorter, very common informal variant with nearly the same meaning.

collocations: having said that, let's move on
having said that, it's a good idea

examples.everyday: The pizza was great. Having said that, I wouldn't wait forty minutes for it again.
examples.professional: The vendor met the uptime target. Having said that, the pricing model still needs a second review.
examples.analytical: The argument is clever. Having said that, it assumes the very conclusion it claims to establish.

nuance.analogy: Like a turn signal in traffic: it warns that the direction is about to change.
common_mistakes: Writing 'Having say that,' which drops the past participle 'said.'
Using it without a clear previous point to qualify, so it sounds abrupt.

senses.definition: Grass cut and dried for use as animal fodder.
Any mix of green leafy plants used for fodder.
senses.example: We stacked the hay in the barn before the rain started.

senses.definition: Cannabis; marijuana.
senses.example: Back in college, my roommate kept a jar of hay under his bed.

senses.definition: A net set around the haunt of an animal, especially a rabbit.
senses.example: The farmer set a hay around the burrow to catch rabbits raiding the garden overnight.

senses.definition: The letter for the h sound in Pitman shorthand.
The Latin letter H.
To cut grasses or herb plants for use as animal fodder.
senses.example: We hayed the north meadow in July before the grass got too tough.

senses.definition: To lay snares for rabbits.
senses.example: Every winter, my grandfather would hay along the fence line to catch rabbits for supper.

core.definition: Dried grass or other plants cut and stored as food for farm animals such as horses and cows.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a long "ay" vowel. Do not add a "y" sound at the end; it is not "hey".

nuance.connotation: Neutral and rural. It is a simple everyday word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "hay" in farm, ranch, and country contexts, and in phrases about horses and barns. Bales of hay are common in fall and summer. In slang, "hay" can also mean marijuana, but this is informal and regional.

distinctions.note: Straw is the dry stalk left after harvest; hay is grass or plants cut and dried for feed.
Grass is growing; hay is cut and dried for storage and feeding.

collocations: make hay while the sun shines

examples.everyday: We need to pick up a few bales of hay before the storm.
examples.professional: The ranch's hay contract was renewed with the local supplier for next season.
examples.analytical: In the parable, the grass and hay represent what is temporary, in contrast to what endures.

nuance.analogy: Hay is like dried leaves stored for winter, ready to feed animals when fresh grass is gone.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hieg, meaning cut grass.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like "hey" with an "h" sound at the end.
Confusing "hay fever" with a fever caused by hay; it is an allergy to pollen.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew chatsir (חָצִיר) means grass or hay, referring to green plants used for food. Psalm 103:15 compares human life to grass and flowers that quickly fade. Proverbs 27:25 describes hay appearing and tender grass shown as part of an ordinary, sustaining harvest. Isaiah 40:6-8 uses the withering of grass as a picture of human frailty, contrasted with the enduring word of God.

hay.etymology: From Middle English *hey*, from Old English *hīeġ*, from **hawi*, from Proto-Germanic **hawją*, from **hawwaną* (“to hew, cut down”).

senses.definition: With a great weight.
senses.example: heavily burdened

senses.definition: To a considerable degree, to a great extent.
senses.example: He relied heavily on the data collected by the others.

senses.definition: In a manner designed for heavy duty.
senses.example: heavily armed soldiers; heavily armored tanks; heavily reinforced walls

senses.definition: So as to be thick or heavy.
senses.example: heavily built young men; his heavily muscled arms

senses.definition: In a labored manner.
senses.example: he breathed heavily

senses.definition: Sadly.
senses.example: "It was all my fault," he replied heavily.

core.definition: To a great extent or degree; very much. Also, with great weight or force.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HEV. The final -ily is a reduced 'ih-lee', not 'eye-lee', and the flapped middle sound is a quick 'v-ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes degree or intensity without judgment, though 'heavily' can suggest a strong or sometimes negative effect, as in 'heavily sedated'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'heavily' with verbs of influence, dependence, weather, and investment, such as 'heavily influenced' or 'it rained heavily.' It sounds natural in both casual and professional speech. Do not use it to mean 'highly' in praise: say 'highly skilled', not 'heavily skilled'.

distinctions.note: 'Highly' means to a high degree or favorably, as in 'highly recommended'. 'Heavily' means to a large extent or with great weight, as in 'heavily taxed'.
'Very much' is a general intensifier used with verbs like 'like' or 'miss'. 'Heavily' is more specific and usually pairs with verbs of influence, load, or weather.

examples.everyday: It rained heavily all afternoon, so we just stayed in and watched movies.
examples.professional: Our Q3 forecast leans heavily on one large client, so I want a downside scenario too.
examples.analytical: Her argument depends heavily on Aquinas's account of causation, and that dependence needs defending.

nuance.analogy: Like a backpack packed with bricks, 'heavily' tells you the weight is great, not just present.
nuance.etymology: From heavy (Old English hefig, 'weighty') plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'heavily' where 'highly' is needed for praise, such as 'heavily skilled' instead of 'highly skilled'.
Pronouncing the ending as 'eye-lee' instead of a reduced 'ih-lee'.

heavily.etymology: From Middle English *hevely*, *hevyliche*, from Old English *hefiġlīċe* (“heavily; grievously”), equivalent to *heavy* + *-ly*.

senses.definition: The state of being heavy; weight, weightiness, force of impact or gravity.

core.definition: The quality of being heavy in weight, or the feeling of sadness, sluggishness, or weight in the body or mind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the next two syllables are quick and reduced. Don't add a long 'ee' to the middle syllable or pronounce the ending as 'ness' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing weight; negative when describing sadness or heaviness of mood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use heaviness for physical weight or for a heavy feeling in the chest or limbs, as in 'a heaviness in my legs.' For emotional sadness, they often prefer heaviness of heart in literary contexts, or simply sadness or grief in everyday speech. It sounds slightly literary in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Weight is the measurable mass, while heaviness can describe the felt sense of weight or sadness.
Sadness is the common everyday word for unhappiness, while heaviness describes a weighed-down feeling in the body or heart.

examples.everyday: After the long flight I felt a heaviness in my legs that wouldn't go away.
examples.professional: The heaviness of the project backlog has made the whole team tired and slow this quarter.
examples.analytical: Scripture often names heaviness of heart not as a sin in itself but as a condition that calls for hope in God.

nuance.analogy: Heaviness is like wet clothing that clings and drags you down, making every step harder.
nuance.etymology: From heavy, from Old English hefig, plus the suffix -ness, meaning 'the state of being'.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle syllable with a long vowel, as in HEV-ee-nus.
Using heaviness for a heavy object, where weight or heavy is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In older English translations, heaviness can mean grief or sorrow of the spirit, which the RSV usually renders as anguish, sorrow, or a downcast heart. Proverbs 12:25 says that anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, while a good word cheers him. The passage shows that inner heaviness is real and that encouraging words can lift it.

heaviness.etymology: From Middle English *hevynesse*, from Old English *hefiġnes* (“heaviness”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to the Hebrew people, language, or culture.

core.definition: Relating to the Hebrew people, their language, or their culture, especially in ancient Israel.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BRAY, the second syllable, and the final syllable is short: 'ik'. Learners often make the first vowel too long or stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a scholarly or descriptive term and carries no negative or positive charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Hebraic mostly in academic, religious, and literary writing, such as Hebraic law or Hebraic poetry. In everyday speech they usually say Hebrew or Jewish, depending on context. Be careful: Hebraic describes a people, language, or culture, while Jewish describes the religion and its adherents today.

distinctions.note: Hebrew is the everyday term for the people, language, or religious tradition. Hebraic is more formal and suggests a culture or style associated with ancient Israel.
Jewish refers today to the religion, people, or community of Judaism. Hebraic is usually used for ancient or biblical contexts and is less common for modern life.

examples.everyday: My friend who studies the Bible says the parables often reflect a Hebraic way of thinking.
examples.professional: Our curriculum includes a unit on Hebraic literature, so the teachers need some background on ancient Israel.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether Paul's ethics are rooted more in Hellenistic philosophy or in a distinctly Hebraic conception of covenant.

nuance.analogy: If Hebrew is the language a house is built in, Hebraic is the architecture that gives the house its style and shape.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin Hebraicus, from Greek Hebraikos, from Hebraios 'Hebrew'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, which makes it sound like 'HEB-ray-ik'.
Using Hebraic to mean religiously Jewish today, where Jewish is the normal American term.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word behind the English Hebrew is 'Ivri' (Hebrew, meaning one from beyond or a descendant of Eber). Genesis 14:13 calls Abram 'the Hebrew', which marks him as an outsider among the peoples of Canaan. Exodus 1:15 refers to the 'Hebrew midwives' in Egypt. Philippians 3:5 describes Paul as 'a Hebrew of Hebrews', emphasizing his thoroughly Hebraic upbringing and identity.

hebraic.etymology: Middle English *Ebrayk,Hebrak,Hebrayke*, a learned borrowing from Late Latin *hebraicus*, borrowed from Byzantine Greek *Ἑβρᾰῐ̈κός*, from Ancient Greek *Ἑβραῖος* (“Hebrew”).

senses.definition: A loyal and trusted follower or subordinate.
A person who supports a political figure chiefly out of selfish interests.
senses.example: The senator's henchman made sure every vote went his way, whatever the cost.

senses.definition: An assistant member of a criminal gang.
senses.example: The gang boss sent his henchman to collect the debt from the shop owner.

core.definition: A loyal follower who carries out orders for a powerful person, often doing dirty or illegal work for personal gain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-man' is reduced to a short 'mun' with no full 'a' vowel, so it sounds like one clear 'ch' sound followed by 'mən'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it usually suggests someone who does a boss's dirty work without much moral independence. Calling someone a henchman is an insult in most contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use henchman in news about crime and politics, and in movies and novels about villains. It can describe a political aide who protects a boss's interests at any cost. In a friendly context it is joking or ironic. Plural is henchmen, and you may hear 'his henchmen' in news stories about gangs or corrupt officials.

distinctions.note: A sidekick is a friendly partner, often admired; a henchman is usually a paid or loyal follower doing questionable work.
A lieutenant has an official or military rank and is neutral in tone; a henchman suggests shady loyalty and is negative.
Minion is informal and often humorous or dismissive; henchman sounds more serious and threatening.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says the mayor's henchmen showed up at the council meeting to pressure people into voting yes.
examples.professional: Our VP's henchman keeps forwarding the emails that blame the data team for missed deadlines.
examples.analytical: A regime may survive for decades by relying on henchmen whose loyalty is bought rather than believed.

nuance.analogy: A henchman is like the hand that holds the knife while the boss gives the order.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English henxman, meaning a groom or attendant of a horse, from Old English hengest, stallion, plus man.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'hen-chee-man' with an extra syllable; it is HENCH-mun.
Using henchman as a neutral job title; it has a negative, criminal or political tone.

henchman.etymology: Middle English *henxman* (“page, attendant”), from Old English **henġestmann,*hengstmann* (“groom”), from *henġest* + *mann*.

senses.definition: To mark (important passages of text), e.g. with a fluorescent marker pen or in a wordprocessor, as a means of memory retention or for later reference.
senses.example: Please highlight the key definitions in the reading before our seminar on Thursday.

senses.definition: To make prominent; emphasize.
senses.example: The report will highlight the rising costs of cloud storage for the executive team.

senses.definition: To be a highlight of.
senses.example: The fireworks highlighted our family reunion, and the kids talked about them for weeks.

senses.definition: To dye (part of the hair) a different color than the rest.
senses.example: She highlighted her hair with honey-blonde streaks before the summer wedding.

senses.definition: To seek the attention of (a user) on IRC by mentioning their name in a message, causing that message to appear highlighted on their screen.
senses.example: Someone highlighted me in the channel, so my client flashed the message in yellow.

senses.definition: An area or a spot in a drawing, painting, or photograph that is strongly illuminated.
senses.example: The photographer adjusted the exposure to keep the highlights on the snowy peaks from washing out.

senses.definition: An especially significant or interesting detail or event or period of time.
senses.example: Meeting my future wife was the highlight of my trip to Spain.

senses.definition: A strand or spot of hair dyed a different color than the rest.
senses.example: Her stylist added a few copper highlights near her face to brighten her dark hair.

core.definition: To mark important text, usually with a colored marker, or to draw special attention to something as important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HY, and the second syllable rhymes with 'light' with a final t. Avoid adding an extra vowel at the end, as in 'high-lite-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly say highlight the important part when marking text, slides, or spreadsheets, and highlight a point in meetings to draw attention to it. As a noun, a highlight is the best part of an event or a show, especially in sports reporting. It is informal enough for everyday talk and standard in work settings.

distinctions.note: Emphasize means to stress a point in speech or writing; highlight can also mean marking text or drawing attention to something visually.
Underline draws a line under words, while highlight usually means coloring the background of text, often with a marker or software tool.

examples.everyday: Can you highlight the best parts of the recipe so we don't miss anything when we shop tomorrow?
examples.professional: Let's highlight the three main risks at the top of the slide so leadership sees them first.
examples.analytical: The author highlights the tension between individual conscience and communal obligation, which becomes central to her argument.

nuance.analogy: Highlighting is like turning on a flashlight in a dark room: it makes certain parts of the text or idea impossible to miss.
nuance.etymology: From high + light, originally from painting, meaning the brightest area of a picture.
common_mistakes: Using 'highlight' for 'hyperlink' or 'link' when talking about web pages.
Saying 'highlight it up' instead of simply 'highlight it'.

conversation.text: I didn't watch the game, but I saw the highlights.
The highlight of the trip was the Grand Canyon.
Highlight the important parts with a yellow marker.

senses.definition: A main public road, especially a multi-lane, high-speed thoroughfare.
senses.example: We drove for six hours on the interstate highway before stopping for lunch in Nebraska.

senses.definition: Any public road.
A way; a path that leads to a certain destiny.
senses.example: You're on a highway to greatness.

senses.definition: Synonym of bus (“common connection for two or more circuits or components”).
senses.example: The firmware routes all memory requests through the processor's highway to reach the peripherals.

senses.definition: To travel on a highway.
senses.example: We highwayed across Kansas all night, stopping only for coffee and gas.

core.definition: A large public road, usually with several lanes and fast traffic, connecting cities or regions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HY, and the second syllable is a diphthong like 'way'. Keep the first vowel long and clear, and don't add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use highway for major roads between cities, often with numbers such as Highway 101. Freeway is common in California and some western cities, and interstate refers to the federal system. Expressway is used for limited-access roads in many regions.

distinctions.note: Freeway is common in some American regions for a limited-access highway with no traffic lights, while highway is the more general term.
Road is any public way; highway suggests a major route for longer-distance travel.

examples.everyday: We took the highway to Chicago, so the drive only took about four hours.
examples.professional: The client's office is right off the highway, so the team can reach the site in fifteen minutes.
examples.analytical: The new highway system transformed American travel by linking distant towns into a national network.

nuance.analogy: A highway is like a main artery in a body: a large route that carries most of the traffic between major areas.
nuance.etymology: From high + way, originally meaning a main public road.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in the highway' instead of 'on the highway', which is the normal American preposition.
Using highway for a short residential street.

highway.etymology: From Middle English *heiȝwai*, *heiȝwei*, from Old English *hēahweġ* (“main road, highway”), corresponding to *high* + *way*.

conversation.text: Take the highway; it's much faster than the back roads.
There's a rest stop off the highway about thirty miles from here.
The speed limit on this highway is seventy.

senses.definition: Someone who perpetrates hoaxes.
senses.example: The hoaxer posted fake photos of a sea monster, and thousands of people shared them before anyone checked.

core.definition: A person who deliberately creates and spreads a false story, object or event in order to fool people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the x a clear ks sound. The final -er is a reduced American r-sound, not a full 'ur' or 'ah.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies deception, though a hoaxer may be seen as mischievous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hoaxer for people who post fake news, create fake photos or start viral pranks. Calling someone a hoaxer is critical, but it is milder than fraudster. In news coverage, people often say the hoaxer or a hoaxer behind the post.

distinctions.note: A prankster plays harmless tricks for fun, while a hoaxer deliberately creates a false claim that others are expected to believe.
An impostor pretends to be a specific person or holds a false role, while a hoaxer invents a false story or object.

examples.everyday: My uncle is such a hoaxer, he sends fake news links to the whole family every morning.
examples.professional: The security team traced the fake outage alert to a hoaxer on an online forum, so we blocked the account.
examples.analytical: A hoaxer depends on the audience's willingness to believe, which is why debunking often fails when people want the story to be true.

nuance.analogy: A hoaxer is like a magician who wants the crowd to believe the illusion is real, not just enjoy the trick.
nuance.etymology: Formed from hoax with the agent suffix -er; hoax is probably a shortening of hocus, from hocus-pocus.
