senses.definition: The prophesied return of Jesus Christ.

core.definition: The Christian belief that Jesus Christ will return to earth in glory at the end of the age to judge and to establish God's kingdom.

pronunciation.tip: Both words carry stress, with the stronger one on COM-. The vowel in 'coming' is /ʌ/ as in 'cup,' not 'oh.' The d in 'second' is often softened before k.

nuance.connotation: Reverent and hopeful in Christian use; it can sound ominous or apocalyptic in popular culture.
nuance.usage_note: Usually written 'Second Coming' with capitals in religious writing. Americans, especially evangelicals and Catholics, use it in church, sermons, and everyday faith talk. Secular speakers may use it jokingly for a much-awaited return, as in 'the second coming of the iPhone.'

distinctions.note: 'Parousia' is the technical Greek term, while 'second coming' is the ordinary English phrase.
'Rapture' refers to believers being taken up to meet Christ, which some Christians distinguish from the Second Coming itself.
'Advent' means a coming in general, and Christians also use it for the season before Christmas.

examples.everyday: My grandmother always said she hoped to see the Second Coming in her lifetime.
examples.professional: Our adult class this week covers what the New Testament teaches about the Second Coming.
examples.analytical: Debates about the timing of the Second Coming have shaped American Protestant identity since the nineteenth century.

nuance.analogy: Like a king who left on a journey and promised to return.
nuance.etymology: 'Second' from Latin secundus 'following' + 'coming' from Old English cuman; the phrase appears in English by the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the second come' instead of 'the Second Coming.'
Confusing it with the Rapture, which is a distinct concept for many Christians.
Pronouncing 'coming' with the vowel of 'home.'
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase 'second coming' does not appear in the RSV, but the idea does. Hebrews 9:28 says Christ will appear a second time to save those awaiting him. Acts 1:11 records the angels telling the disciples that Jesus will return in the same way he ascended. Matthew 24:30 describes the Son of man coming on the clouds with power and glory.

senses.definition: Promoting the good of one division, department or subgroup over that of the whole.
senses.example: Sectionalism hurt the national party when delegates from each region blocked compromise.

senses.definition: Promoting the good of one region over that of the nation.
senses.example: Sectionalism is tearing the country apart. Everyone wants the other regions to do the work and pay the taxes while they reap the benefits.

core.definition: Loyalty to one's own region, group, or department that puts its interests ahead of those of the larger whole.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The -ism ending is a weak 'iz-um' with the final syllable reduced, so do not say 'liz-ISM' with a strong last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a narrow focus on local or group interests at the expense of the wider community.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sectionalism in political history, politics, and organizational discussions, for example when a company's departments compete for budget. In everyday talk, people more often say they are only looking out for their own state or team. The word can be used sharply, so it is best reserved for serious discussion rather than casual teasing.

distinctions.note: Regionalism can be positive, meaning pride or special attention to a region's culture; sectionalism is negative and suggests putting a region above the nation.
Tribalism refers to loyalty to a group defined by identity or kinship, while sectionalism refers to loyalty to a geographic region or organizational division.

examples.everyday: My uncle has so much sectionalism that he only roots for teams from his own town.
examples.professional: Sectionalism between product teams slowed the release by several months.
examples.analytical: Sectionalism in the early republic weakened national unity by placing regional economic interests above the common good.

nuance.analogy: Sectionalism is like a family in which each room cares only about its own comfort and nobody cares whether the whole house is in good repair.
nuance.etymology: From sectional, from section, from Latin sectio 'a cutting', plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using sectionalism to mean any regional pride; the word is usually negative.
Confusing sectionalism with sectarianism, which refers to religious or doctrinal divisions.
Mispronouncing the stress on the final syllable.

senses.definition: To accompany a guest to the door when he or she leaves.
senses.example: Please see our guest out.

senses.definition: To continue something until completion; to watch an activity develop to a conclusion.
senses.example: I'll never give up. I'm going to see this thing out.

core.definition: To stay with something until it ends, such as a meeting, a difficult period or a project; also to walk a guest to the door.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on out, with a lighter secondary stress on see. Pronounce out with the diphthong ow, and do not reduce it, because the particle carries the meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can suggest endurance or determination when used for hard situations, and politeness when used for guests.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say see out to mean finishing something through to its end, often when it has been hard or long, such as a contract or a bad winter. For guests, saying I'll see you out is a polite, slightly formal way to offer to walk someone to the door. A natural reply is Thanks, I'll see myself out or Sure, I'll get the door.

distinctions.note: See off means to go to a station, airport or port to say goodbye to someone departing, while see out means to stay until something ends.
Stick it out is more informal and emphasizes enduring discomfort, while see out is more neutral and often refers to completing a project or term.

examples.everyday: Thanks for coming over tonight, let me see you out before the rain starts.
examples.professional: We have two sprints left, so I'll see the migration out before I hand the service to the operations team.
examples.analytical: Historians still debate whether the regime could see out the economic crisis or whether its legitimacy collapsed well before the final collapse.

nuance.analogy: Like staying in your seat until the closing credits end, you are not leaving before the story is finished.
nuance.etymology: Combines see, from Old English seon, with out, from Old English ut.
common_mistakes: Putting the object after out in a way that sounds wrong, saying see out him instead of see him out; the pronoun goes between the two words.
Confusing see out with see off, which means saying goodbye at a departure point rather than finishing something.

senses.definition: Of a liquid or other substance, or a container holding it: to be boiled (vigorously); to become boiling hot.
senses.example: Let the broth seethe gently on the stove for twenty minutes before you add the rice.

senses.definition: Of a liquid, vapor, etc. or a container holding it: to foam or froth in an agitated manner, as if boiling.
senses.example: The soapy water began to seethe and foam as the dishwasher filled.

senses.definition: Of a person: to be in an agitated or angry mental state, often in a way that is not obvious to others.
senses.example: Although she smiled through dinner, she seethed quietly about her brother's comments all evening.

senses.definition: Of a place: to be filled with many people or things moving about actively; to buzz with activity; also, of people or things: to move about actively in a crowd or group.
senses.example: The trade floor seethed with traders shouting orders as the market opened.

senses.definition: Of a place: to have inhabitants in an angry or disaffected mood; to be in a state of unrest.
senses.example: By the spring of 1848, the provincial towns seethed with resentment against the crown.

senses.definition: To overboil (something) so that it loses its flavor or texture; hence, to cause (the body, the mind, the spirit, etc.) to become dull through too much alcoholic drink or heat.
senses.example: Don't let the pasta seethe too long, or it will turn mushy and lose its flavor.

senses.definition: To soak (something) in a liquid; to drench, to steep.
senses.example: Seethe the dried figs in warm brandy overnight so they plump up for the cake.

senses.definition: To boil (something); especially, to cook (food) by boiling or stewing; also, to keep (something) boiling.
senses.example: Seethe the lentils in salted water until they are soft enough to mash.

senses.definition: A state of boiling or frothing; ebullition, seething; hence, extreme heat; much activity.
senses.example: The kitchen was in a seethe of steam and shouting as the holiday dinner rush began.

core.definition: To be extremely angry or agitated, often silently; or, of a liquid, to boil or foam vigorously.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable, and 'th' is voiced, like the th in 'they'. Do not make it a voiceless th as in 'think'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes intense anger or resentment, usually held in rather than shouted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'seethe' mainly in writing and in serious conversation about feelings. It is often followed by 'with' or 'inside'. Saying 'I was seething' in casual speech is fine, but it sounds more dramatic than 'I was really mad'.

distinctions.note: 'Fume' emphasizes visible or simmering anger; 'seethe' suggests anger that is intense and boiling inside.
'Boil' is the common word for hot water; 'seethe' is more literary and can describe agitated crowds or emotions.

examples.everyday: He was seething when the mechanic charged him twice for the same repair.
examples.professional: The team was seething over the unfair reassignment, though nobody said so in the meeting.
examples.analytical: The novel's narrator seethes with resentment, and the prose itself seems to boil under pressure.

nuance.analogy: Like a pot that is boiling hard inside even before the lid rattles.
nuance.etymology: From Old English seoðan, 'to boil'.
common_mistakes: Using 'seethe' for mild annoyance; it implies strong anger.
Pronouncing the th as voiceless, which makes it sound like 'seeth' in 'teeth' with the wrong sound.

seethe.etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English *sethen*, *seeth* (“to boil, seethe; to cook; etc.”), from Old English *sēoþan* (“to boil, seethe; to cook; etc.”), from **seuþan*, from Proto-Germanic **seuþaną* (“to boil, seethe”), from Proto-Indo-European…

senses.definition: Of or relating to a seigneur or to seigneurialism.
Befitting a seigneur.

core.definition: Relating to a seigneur, a feudal lord, or to the system of feudal lordship and its rights and privileges.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on YOOR. The first syllable sounds like 'sane', and the spelling 'gn' is pronounced like 'ny', so the word is not 'SAYN-yur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in historical writing; can suggest grandeur, privilege or aristocratic authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet seigneurial in history, French-Canadian studies, or literary description of manors and estates. In everyday speech they would say 'feudal' or 'manorial.' It is specialized and rare in conversation.

distinctions.note: Feudal is broader, describing the whole medieval social and land system; seigneurial focuses on the lord's rights and status.
Manorial refers to the manor as an estate; seigneurial refers to the lord and his privileges, especially under the French system.

examples.everyday: The old stone house still has the grandeur of a seigneurial estate.
examples.professional: Our history lecture contrasts seigneurial land tenure with later freehold systems.
examples.analytical: The Quebec seigneurial system shaped rural life long after the lords' legal powers were abolished.

nuance.analogy: Like a feudal castle with its own rules and dues, where one local lord governed an entire valley.
nuance.etymology: From Old French seigneur, from Latin senior, meaning elder.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in SAYN-yur-ee-al; the stress falls on YOOR.
Confusing seigneur with the English word senior; seigneur means a feudal lord.

senses.definition: Relating to seismology.

core.definition: Relating to seismology, the scientific study of earthquakes and ground vibrations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAH, where the o is pronounced like 'ah' as in cot, not 'aw'. The first syllable has a weaker secondary stress, and the final -al is light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it sounds scientific and formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seismological in science writing, research papers and job titles, as in seismological data or the Seismological Society of America. In casual speech people just talk about earthquakes or quake research. Keep the word for documents and presentations.

distinctions.note: Seismic is broader and can describe anything involving earth vibrations or dramatic shaking; seismological refers specifically to the scientific field.
Geophysical covers the whole physics of the Earth; seismological narrows the focus to earthquakes and vibrations.

examples.everyday: My neighbor works for the state, and her seismological team checks the fault lines near our town every spring.
examples.professional: The seismological group needs the sensor logs before we can finalize the hazard report for the county.
examples.analytical: Seismological models assume that stress builds slowly along faults, which makes simple predictions of the next quake very difficult.

nuance.analogy: A seismological model is like a weather forecast for the ground, built from past patterns and current measurements.
nuance.etymology: From seismology plus the adjective suffix -ical.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle o as in law (seismo-LAW-jical); American speech uses the ah sound.
Confusing seismological (the science) with seismic (the shaking itself).

senses.definition: The state of being excessively pleased with oneself; smugness.
A feeling of fulfillment or contentment with respect to one's own accomplishments or situation.
senses.example: He spoke with quiet self-satisfaction after finishing the marathon in under four hours.

core.definition: Excessive pleasure in your own achievements, often with a smug lack of awareness of your faults or of what remains undone.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress falls on the -FAC- syllable, with secondary stress on self and sat. Don't say the older-looking SAT-is-fac-tion; the 'is' reduces to a quick 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative when it means smugness. In a neutral sense it can mean quiet contentment, so context decides.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for smug pride, often when criticizing a politician, boss or colleague who seems pleased with a flawed result. For calm contentment with a good life, they usually say satisfaction or contentment. Calling a friend's happiness self-satisfaction could sound critical.

distinctions.note: Self-confidence is a healthy belief in your abilities, while self-satisfaction is complacency that has stopped checking itself.
Pride can be a healthy sense of accomplishment, while self-satisfaction usually suggests complacency, often unearned.
Contentment is calm peace with what you have, while self-satisfaction is an inflated, self-congratulating view of yourself.

examples.everyday: He had this self-satisfaction after winning one game, like the whole season was already over.
examples.professional: The leadership deck had a tone of self-satisfaction about the quarter that ignored the three projects we missed.
examples.analytical: Many moral writers warn that self-satisfaction can pass for virtue, since a person who feels finished has stopped growing.

nuance.analogy: Like a student who stops studying after one good test, self-satisfaction mistakes a single success for mastery.
nuance.etymology: From self plus satisfaction, from Latin satisfacere, meaning to do enough, from satis 'enough' and facere 'to do'.
common_mistakes: Using self-satisfaction for ordinary happiness; in American English it usually sounds critical.
Stressing only the first syllable, SELF, and ignoring the main stress on FAC.

senses.definition: An extendable monopod arm onto which a smartphone or camera can be mounted in order to take wide-angle photographs of oneself.
senses.example: I clipped my phone onto a selfie stick to capture the whole group at the concert.

core.definition: A telescoping pole that holds a smartphone or camera, letting you take wide-angle photos of yourself and a group.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STICK, and selfie ends in a long ee sound, not ay. The -lf in self is a clean f with no t after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; playful, though sometimes teased as vain or touristy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use selfie stick in everyday talk, especially at tourist sites, concerts and family trips. Some parks, museums and stadiums ban them, so you may see the term on signs. Friends may tease someone for using one, but it is an ordinary object. A typical request is 'Can you hold the phone on the selfie stick?'

distinctions.note: A tripod has three legs and stands on its own, while a selfie stick is a handheld pole for shooting at arm's length.
A gimbal is a motorized stabilizer for smooth video, while a selfie stick is a simple pole without motion correction.

examples.everyday: Hold on, let me grab the selfie stick so we can get the whole group in the photo at the Grand Canyon.
examples.professional: The marketing team wants a selfie stick for the booth demo, so attendees can capture themselves with the product.
examples.analytical: The selfie stick extends the photographer's arm into the frame, so the self-portrait becomes a deliberate statement about perspective and presence.

nuance.analogy: Like a long arm you can extend to take your own portrait from a distance.
nuance.etymology: From selfie, a casual shortening of self-portrait, plus stick.
common_mistakes: Spelling it selfy stick or self stick; the word is selfie.
Stressing the second syllable of selfie (self-FEE) instead of putting the main stress on the last word.

senses.definition: To engage in the process of short selling (selling a stock one does not own on the premise of the stock's price going down).
senses.example: Her analyst warned that traders who sell short could lose everything if the stock rebounds.

senses.definition: To underestimate the value of something; to understate its value.
senses.example: You're selling it short by not mentioning its bonus features.

core.definition: To underestimate the value or ability of someone or something; to sell yourself short means to doubt your own worth.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on SHORT. Pronounce the American 'r' clearly, and do not drop it as in British speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests that someone or something is being valued too low, often in a way that causes harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Don't sell yourself short' to encourage someone to aim high or believe in their abilities. In finance, 'sell short' has a separate technical meaning, betting that a stock will fall. A natural reply to the encouragement is 'Thanks, I'll try.' The phrase is common in conversation, coaching and business.

distinctions.note: Undersell means to charge less than competitors, which is a pricing decision, while sell short means to undervalue someone or something.
Undervalue is a neutral, general word for giving too low a worth, while sell short is more idiomatic and often used for self-doubt.

examples.everyday: Don't sell yourself short. You'd be great at that job if you applied.
examples.professional: We sold the project short by promising a two-week timeline before we understood the data.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the report sells short the costs borne by workers in the global supply chain.

nuance.analogy: Like pricing a valuable painting as if it were a poster.
common_mistakes: Confusing the everyday meaning with the finance meaning of 'short selling.'
Using 'undersell' for undervaluing a person's abilities, which sounds unnatural.

senses.definition: A beverage or ingredient thereof, consisting of plain carbonated water; often for use in mixing with alcohol, cordials, and juices.

core.definition: Plain carbonated water with no added flavor, often used for drinking or mixing with alcohol and juice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WA in water and give seltzer a weaker secondary stress. In General American, the t in water is a quick flap that sounds like a soft d, so say WAW-der, not WAW-ter.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It describes a simple beverage without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say seltzer alone once the context is clear, but seltzer water is more explicit, especially when ordering or shopping. People mix it with whiskey, gin, or juice for a light drink. Use it instead of soda when you mean unflavored bubbly water.

distinctions.note: Soda water is the British and some American term for seltzer or club soda, so it is less common in American stores.
Sparkling water is a general category that can include mineral water; seltzer water is artificially carbonated plain water.
Tonic water is sweetened and bitter from quinine, so it tastes very different.

examples.everyday: I'll have a whiskey and seltzer water, hold the sugar.
examples.professional: Please add seltzer water to the catering order for the reception.
examples.analytical: The term seltzer water designates plain carbonated water, which distinguishes it from flavored or mineral waters.

nuance.analogy: Seltzer water is like a blank canvas for a drink: the bubbles are there, but the flavor comes from what you add.
nuance.etymology: Seltzer comes from Selters, a town in Germany; water is the general word for the liquid.
common_mistakes: Calling it soda, which in American English usually means a sweet soft drink.
Flattening the t in water into a hard t sound, when the American flap is softer.

seltzer-water.etymology: From the waters of Selters, Germany, which are naturally carbonated.

senses.definition: The condition of being sequential.

core.definition: The quality or condition of being sequential, meaning arranged or happening in a fixed order, one thing after another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AL, the fourth syllable, which carries the main stress. The earlier syllables are light and reduced, so avoid giving each syllable equal weight.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise abstract term.
nuance.usage_note: Sequentiality is rare in American English and used mainly in computing, philosophy, linguistics and formal analysis. Most speakers would say 'the order of steps' or 'the sequence of events' instead. The word is useful when you want to name the quality itself.

distinctions.note: A sequence is the ordered set itself, while sequentiality is the abstract quality of being ordered in this way.
Succession is the act of following one after another, often used for rulers or events, while sequentiality is an abstract property.
Consecutiveness stresses an unbroken run, while sequentiality stresses order without requiring an unbroken run.

examples.everyday: The recipe has no real sequentiality, so you can start the sauce whenever you want.
examples.professional: We discussed whether the pipeline's sequentiality was necessary or just a leftover from the old design.
examples.analytical: Narrative sequentiality can mislead readers into assuming causation where there is only chronology.

nuance.analogy: Sequentiality is like a row of dominoes: the quality of falling in a fixed order, one after another.
nuance.etymology: From sequential plus -ity, from Latin sequi, 'to follow.'
common_mistakes: Using sequentiality when the simpler word sequence is enough.
Putting stress on the first syllable instead of AL.

senses.definition: The process of serializing.
The process or action of converting something in a serial or into serial form.
senses.example: The publisher's serialization of the novel ran in weekly installments through the summer.

core.definition: In computing, the process of converting an object or data structure into a format that can be stored or sent and later rebuilt.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on ZAY, the syllable before -shun. Keep the 'ee' in 'sir' and the 'ai' in 'lye' clear, and don't reduce the middle syllables into one blur.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a routine engineering process, not a negative or emotional idea.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use serialization in software, data engineering, and machine learning when they discuss saving models, sending messages, or converting objects to JSON or binary. It is not used for TV episodes in these contexts; for that, Americans say the show was released in seasons or episodes. Engineers often shorten it to serialize in speech.

distinctions.note: Encoding is a general word for converting text or data into another representation; serialization specifically means turning structured objects into a stream of bytes or text.
Deserialization is the reverse process, rebuilding the original object from the serialized form.

examples.everyday: My laptop app uses serialization to save my settings so they come back when I restart.
examples.professional: Our API team switched to Protocol Buffers because the serialization was much faster and smaller than JSON.
examples.analytical: Serialization exposes a design tension between preserving an object's internal structure and keeping an external format stable across versions.

nuance.analogy: Serialization is like packing furniture into boxes for a move: you take the shape apart into a sequence that fits, and later unpack it into the same piece.
nuance.etymology: From serialize, from serial (Latin series, row or sequence), plus the suffix -ation.
common_mistakes: Using serialization for the TV sense of series; in tech it means turning an object into a storable format.
Stressing the first syllable ('SIR-ee-uh-lye-ZAY-shun' is correct, but many learners drop the -ee- and say 'sir-ul-ih-ZAY-shun').

senses.definition: Notched or cut like a saw.
senses.example: That knife has a serrated blade.

senses.definition: Having a row of sharp or tooth-like projections.
senses.example: Maple leaves have serrated edges.

core.definition: Having a row of small, sharp, saw-like teeth along an edge, like a bread knife.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -ated ending is weak, so say 'SEHR-ay-tid' with a short final vowel, not 'SEHR-ay-ted'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it describes a physical feature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use serrated in everyday talk about knives, scissors, and tools, such as 'Use the serrated knife for the bread.' It is also common in product descriptions and cooking. It is less casual than 'toothy' but more common than the technical 'serrate'.

distinctions.note: Jagged means irregular and rough, with no pattern; serrated implies a regular row of teeth like a saw.
Smooth describes an edge with no teeth, the typical contrast when you choose between knife types.

examples.everyday: Use the serrated knife for the bread, because the smooth one just squashes it.
examples.professional: The serrated edge on the cutter reduces slipping when it goes through the packaging film.
examples.analytical: The serrated blade distributes pressure across many contact points, which changes how it cuts fibrous material.

nuance.analogy: A serrated edge is like a row of tiny shark teeth, each one grabbing and sawing.
nuance.etymology: From serrate, from Latin serratus, 'sawlike', plus the English past-participle ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'ray' with stress, instead of 'SEHR-ay-tid'.
Confusing the adjective with the verb form; both exist, but in everyday speech the adjective is far more common.

senses.definition: To cause to begin to burn.
To arouse passionate feelings in.
senses.example: You set my heart on fire.

core.definition: To cause something to begin to burn, sometimes by accident, or to excite strong emotion in people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FIRE. The word on is weak and often sounds like 'ahn' or 'un' in speech. The final er is a reduced vowel with r coloring, so fire sounds like 'FYE-er'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative for literal fires, positive for the figurative sense of exciting a crowd.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for literal fires, often accidental: 'The candle set the curtains on fire.' The figurative sense, as in 'The speech set the crowd on fire,' is very common and positive. For deliberate arson, many speakers prefer set fire to. A natural reply is 'Wow, was anyone hurt?'

distinctions.note: Set fire to usually implies deliberate action; set on fire can describe either an accident or an intentional act and is more everyday.
Ignite is technical or formal, used in chemistry or engines; set on fire is everyday language.
Catch fire means begin burning without anyone causing it; set on fire requires a cause.

examples.everyday: The toaster sparked and nearly set the kitchen towel on fire.
examples.professional: A faulty battery set the test rig on fire, so we shut down the lab until the cause was found.
examples.analytical: The metaphor sets the reader's imagination on fire, but it obscures the logic of the argument it is meant to support.

nuance.analogy: Like a spark landing on dry paper: one small moment leads to a blaze.
nuance.etymology: From set (to put into a state) and fire (Old English fyr), meaning to put fire into something.
common_mistakes: Saying set to fire; the correct forms are set on fire or set fire to.
Using the phrase only for literal fire and missing the figurative sense, which is very common in American speech.

senses.definition: A suspension of water and solid waste, transported by sewers to be disposed of or processed.
senses.example: Untreated sewage can pollute rivers.

core.definition: Liquid and solid human waste carried away from homes and businesses through pipes and sewers for treatment or disposal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The letters 'ew' sound like the oo in 'soon', not the ee in 'see', and the final syllable is a weak ij, not 'age' with a long a.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It refers to waste, so it is unpleasant and often connected to pollution, smell or health risks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sewage for the waste material itself, especially in news about floods, treatment plants or contamination. Plumbers, city workers and homeowners also use it in everyday talk about backups and basements. It is not a British-only word, so no American alternative is needed, though wastewater is used in technical contexts.

distinctions.note: Sewage is the waste material, while a sewer is the pipe or channel that carries it.
Wastewater is a broader term that includes industrial waste and storm runoff. Sewage refers specifically to waste from people.
Effluent is liquid discharged from a source, often after partial treatment. Sewage is the raw or mixed waste carried through sewers.

examples.everyday: After the flood, the basement smelled like sewage, so we called a plumber right away.
examples.professional: The city's sewage treatment plant needs a capacity upgrade before the new subdivision opens next year.
examples.analytical: Public health history suggests that separating drinking water from sewage did more to reduce disease than any single medical advance.

nuance.analogy: Sewage is like the leftover mess of a large household, collected and sent away so it does not spoil the rest of the house.
nuance.etymology: Formed from sewer plus -age; sewer comes from Anglo-French seuwere, from Latin exaquare 'to drain off'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel like ee (SEE-ij) or the second syllable like age (SOO-ayj).
Using sewage and sewer as if they were the same thing, when one is the waste and the other is the pipe.

sewage.etymology: From *sewer* + *age* or from *sew* (“to drain or draw off water”) + *-age*.

core.definition: The Jewish harvest festival held fifty days after Passover, also called the Feast of Weeks, which commemorates the giving of the Torah at Sinai.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the last syllable, VOOT. Many English speakers add an extra vowel at the end, so keep it to one clean syllable after the stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and religious; it is a respectful term used in Jewish contexts and in interfaith or cultural conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this Hebrew name mostly in Jewish communities, synagogues, and news about holidays. In casual talk, many people say Shavuot as it is or describe it as the holiday seven weeks after Passover. Christians more often connect it with Pentecost, so they may ask about it in a Bible study.

distinctions.note: Pentecost is the Christian name for the feast, drawn from the Greek word for fiftieth, and it marks the coming of the Holy Spirit in Acts 2; Shavuot is the Jewish name for the same timing.
Passover comes first, in spring, and celebrates the Exodus from Egypt, while Shavuot follows fifty days later.

examples.everyday: My neighbor invited us to a dairy dinner for Shavuot, so we brought dessert.
examples.professional: Our company closes early before Shavuot, so please plan your deliveries for the day before.
examples.analytical: In Exodus and Deuteronomy the feast is called the Feast of Weeks, and its later association with the giving of the Torah shows how the agricultural festival took on a historical meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like Thanksgiving, Shavuot combines a harvest celebration with a central story that shapes the community's identity.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew shavuot, meaning weeks, referring to the seven weeks counted from Passover.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as SHAH-vuht; the stress belongs on the last syllable.
Confusing Shavuot with Sukkot, a different autumn festival.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew shavuot means weeks. Leviticus 23:15-16 requires counting seven weeks from the offering of the sheaf and then presenting a new grain offering on the fiftieth day. Exodus 34:22 and Deuteronomy 16:10 call it the Feast of Weeks and link it with the wheat harvest.

core.definition: A Hebrew man named as the father of Zerubbabel, who led the Jews returning from Babylon to rebuild the Temple.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on AL, the second syllable. Americans often say the t as a clear t, not a flap, and the final el is a light syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a name used in religious and historical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this name in Bible study, sermons, or history of the Second Temple. In everyday talk it would not come up unless a conversation is about the Bible or Jewish history.

distinctions.note: Salathiel is the Greek-influenced form used in Matthew 1:12 and Luke 3:27 in the RSV, while Shealtiel is the form used in Ezra and Haggai.

examples.everyday: My Bible study leader mentioned Shealtiel, the father of Zerubbabel, when we read Haggai.
examples.professional: For the sermon on rebuilding, I cited Shealtiel's line as the link to Zerubbabel's leadership.
examples.analytical: The genealogy of Shealtiel and Zerubbabel anchors the Persian-period restoration of the Davidic line within the Second Temple community.

nuance.analogy: Like a family tree branch that connects two famous relatives, Shealtiel links Zerubbabel to the earlier history of the Jewish people.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Sheʾaltiʾel, meaning I asked God, or God is my request.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as SHEE-al-tee-el.
Confusing Shealtiel with Salathiel, which appears in the New Testament genealogies.
nuance.biblical_note: Shealtiel appears as the father of Zerubbabel in Ezra 3:2 and as the name in Haggai 1:1, where he is the father of the governor Zerubbabel. Ezra 3:2 links Shealtiel with the rebuilding of the altar after the exile.

senses.definition: An area hosting multiple retail stores, especially one with outdoor common areas.
senses.example: We met for coffee at the shopping center near the highway exit.

core.definition: A group of stores built together in one area, often with a shared parking lot and sometimes open-air walkways.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second word, center, while shopping has a lighter stress. Keep the e short as in bet, not a long ee, and let the -er be a reduced rhotic sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a place for everyday errands and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shopping center for a group of stores, often with a grocery store or pharmacy as the anchor, in a plaza along a road. Americans spell it center, while British English uses shopping centre and often means an indoor complex. People often shorten it to the center. A single row of stores in one building is more often called a strip mall.

distinctions.note: A mall is usually a larger, enclosed building with an interior walkway, while a shopping center is often open-air with separate store entrances.
A strip mall is a row of stores in one long building with a shared lot and no central walkway.
An outlet center sells discounted goods from brands, usually in an open-air layout, and is a specific type of shopping center.

examples.everyday: Let's meet at the shopping center by the Target and grab coffee first.
examples.professional: The planning board approved the redevelopment of the old shopping center on Route 9.
examples.analytical: Shopping centers reflect a postwar suburban model in which car access shaped where stores and parking were placed.

nuance.analogy: A shopping center is like a small village square built for cars, where the stores face a shared parking lot.
nuance.etymology: Compound of shopping (from shop) and center (from Latin centrum).
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling centre in American writing.
Saying in the shopping center when you mean one store; a shopping center is a group of stores, so say at the store for a single shop.

senses.definition: The amount that can be moved at once with a shovel.
senses.example: One shovelful of dirt makes a molehill; a million shovelfuls make a mountain.

core.definition: The amount of material that a shovel can hold or move at one time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SHOV, and the suffix '-ful' is a weak syllable in fast speech, so it can sound like 'fuhl'. Do not add an extra syllable between 'shov' and 'el'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive, used for everyday measurement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'a shovelful of dirt' or 'a shovelful of snow' when describing how much is moved in one scoop. The word is common in gardening, construction and yard work. It is used with 'of' for the material.

distinctions.note: A scoop is a general word for an amount taken up with a spoon, ice cream scoop or hands, while a shovelful refers to a shovel.
A bucketful is the amount a bucket holds; a shovelful is the amount a shovel moves in one motion.

examples.everyday: I'll grab a shovelful of mulch for the flower bed before the rain starts.
examples.professional: The excavation log counts each shovelful of fill as one unit, so the crew should record the total count daily.
examples.analytical: A single shovelful of soil can contain billions of microbes, which makes sampling design a serious methodological problem.

nuance.analogy: Like a single bite of food: it is one manageable portion of a larger task.
nuance.etymology: From 'shovel' plus the suffix '-ful', meaning as much as a shovel holds.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as 'full' with a strong vowel instead of a reduced one.
Writing 'shovelfull' with two l's, which is a common spelling error.
Saying 'a shovel of dirt' when 'a shovelful of dirt' is the usual phrase.

senses.definition: A secondary road; a road that is not intended for heavy traffic.
senses.example: Traffic was horrible on the main roads, but she knew all the back roads and side streets, and managed to get there quickly.

core.definition: A secondary road, usually narrower and quieter than a main road, that branches off or runs alongside it.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun the main stress falls on SIDE, not on street, so say SYDE-street rather than syde-STREET. The t in street is a clear, aspirated t, not a flap, and the r after it is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it simply describes a type of road with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use side street for any smaller road off a main road, especially in neighborhoods and downtown, as in turn onto a side street. For a quiet residential road, people often say residential street. A side street is a public road, not the sidewalk, which Americans call the sidewalk and Britons call the pavement.

distinctions.note: A main road carries most of the traffic, while a side street branches from it and carries much less.
An alley is a narrow lane behind or between buildings, while a side street is a full public road.

examples.everyday: Just turn left on the side street after the gas station and you will see the house.
examples.professional: The delivery trucks cannot get in from the main road, so we will unload from the side street.
examples.analytical: Traffic studies often separate arterial roads from side streets, since they carry very different volumes of traffic.

nuance.analogy: A side street is like a tributary feeding a river: smaller and quieter, but connected to the main flow.
nuance.etymology: Side comes from Old English side, meaning flank; street comes from Latin strata, a paved road.
common_mistakes: Saying side street when you mean the sidewalk, the walkway beside the road.
Stressing STREET in the compound, which makes it sound like two separate words rather than one place name.

senses.definition: In the sixth place; sixth in a row.

core.definition: In the sixth place, used to introduce the sixth point in a formal list of reasons or arguments.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, then say 'th' and 'lee' quickly. The word sounds formal, so Americans rarely pronounce it with extra vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to formal; it sounds deliberate and old-fashioned in speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use sixthly in everyday speech, preferring 'sixth' or 'finally' as the last point in a list. You will see it mainly in older sermons, academic argument, or formal writing. If you use it casually, it may sound like a joke.

distinctions.note: Lastly signals the final point in a list; sixthly signals a specific position in a numbered sequence.
Sixth is an adjective or noun for position; sixthly is an adverb that introduces a point in a sequence.

examples.everyday: Firstly, pick up milk; secondly, call the plumber; sixthly, please tell me you fed the dog.
examples.professional: We have five open issues; sixthly, the budget forecast still ignores the new contract.
examples.analytical: Sixthly, the argument assumes that moral obligation tracks consequences, a premise it never establishes.

nuance.analogy: Sixthly is like a numbered sign on a long hallway, marking how far you have come.
nuance.etymology: Formed from sixth plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using sixthly in casual conversation where 'finally' or 'sixth' is more natural.
Pronouncing it as 'sixtly', dropping the 'h' sound in the middle.

senses.definition: To move or run away quickly.
To spill; to scatter.
senses.example: Don't skedaddle the beans all over the kitchen floor, young man.

senses.definition: The act of running away; a scurrying off.
senses.example: The thief made a quick skedaddle out the back door when the sirens started.

core.definition: To run away quickly, often in an informal or playful way, to leave a place fast.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: skih-DAD-uhl. The final -dle is a syllabic l, not 'dal', and the vowel in the stressed syllable is short, as in 'dad'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to humorous; it suggests a quick, somewhat comical departure, sometimes a retreat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use skedaddle casually and often humorously, for kids leaving, a crowd scattering, or a guest heading home. It sounds informal and a little old-fashioned or folksy. Telling someone 'Skedaddle!' is an informal way to say get out of here, which can be playful or rude depending on your tone.

distinctions.note: Scram is a blunter command to leave immediately; skedaddle is more playful and describes running off quickly.
Flee is formal and serious, used for escaping danger; skedaddle is informal and lighter.

examples.everyday: The rain's coming, so let's skedaddle before we get soaked.
examples.professional: When the budget review turned tense, the vendors quietly skedaddled from the meeting.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the executives skedaddled from responsibility instead of explaining the failures.

nuance.analogy: Like a squirrel that scatters when someone opens the door: quick, sudden, and not planned.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; it appeared as American slang around the 1860s, during the Civil War era.
common_mistakes: Using it in serious formal writing where flee or depart fits better
Stressing the first syllable, as in SKED-uh-dal
Spelling it skeedaddle; the standard spelling is skedaddle, though skidaddle is also recorded

senses.definition: A connection that lets information bypass one or more layers; a residual connection is one kind.
senses.example: Adding a skip connection let the gradients flow directly to earlier layers.

core.definition: In a neural network, a link that lets input or information bypass one or more layers and join a later layer directly.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'nec' in 'connection', while 'skip' has secondary stress. The 'o' in 'connection' is a reduced schwa, so say 'kuh-NEK-shun', not 'kon-NEK-shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is a technical term used in deep learning and computer vision research, in papers, code and architecture discussions. Engineers say 'add a skip connection' or 'the model uses skip connections.' It is not used in everyday conversation, and a residual connection is a specific type of skip connection.

distinctions.note: A residual connection adds the input to the output of a block; a skip connection is the broader term that covers that and other bypass links.
Shortcut connection is a common synonym in many papers, especially in ResNet-style architectures; the two terms are often interchangeable.

examples.professional: We added a skip connection from the encoder to the decoder, which helped the model keep fine details.
examples.analytical: The skip connection preserves the original signal, so each layer learns only the residual correction rather than the full mapping.

nuance.analogy: A skip connection is like an express lane on a highway: traffic can bypass the local stops and still arrive at the same destination.
nuance.etymology: 'Skip' from Middle English skippen, 'connection' from Latin connectere, to bind together; the compound is a modern technical coinage.
common_mistakes: Confusing skip connections with skipping layers during training, which is a different idea called layer dropping.
Pronouncing 'connection' as 'kon-NEK-shun' with a full vowel in the first syllable.

conversation.text: A skip connection passes information past one or more layers to a later point in the network.
U-Net uses skip connections to carry fine spatial detail from the encoder to the decoder.

senses.definition: Including or given to slang.
senses.example: His slangy speech was almost uncomprehensible to anyone over the age of 18.

senses.definition: (dated) Loud in dress, manner, and conversation; flashy, vulgar.
senses.example: Aunt Ruth frowned at his slangy plaid jacket and his loud, boastful talk at the dinner table.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Full of slang; using informal, colloquial words and expressions in speech or writing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SLANG, and the final -y is a light 'ee' sound. Do not add a hard g after the ng.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative to neutral; it usually describes writing or speech as too casual for the setting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slangy mainly in writing and criticism, such as a reviewer describing a novel's dialogue as slangy. In conversation people more often say 'slangy' about someone's speech in a teasing way or say 'casual.' It is rarely a compliment in formal contexts.

distinctions.note: Informal is a general term for relaxed style; slangy specifically means heavy use of slang words.
Colloquial describes everyday spoken language; slangy describes language that goes further into slang and can sound more playful or edgy.

examples.everyday: My grandmother said my texts were too slangy and asked me to write whole sentences.
examples.professional: The editor marked the draft as slangy and asked the writers to rewrite the marketing copy in a more professional tone.
examples.analytical: Critics often describe the novel's dialogue as slangy, a choice that signals the characters' class and generation.

nuance.analogy: A slangy sentence is like a casual outfit with sneakers and a hoodie: comfortable and expressive, but not right for every occasion.
nuance.etymology: From slang plus the suffix -y, meaning full of or like.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle sound as 'slan-jee' with a hard g.
Using slangy to mean fashionable or flashy, a dated sense that Americans rarely use today.

senses.definition: To move about smoothly and from side to side.
To slide.
senses.example: The garter snake would slither across the wet rocks toward the creek.

senses.definition: A limestone rubble.
senses.example: The field survey recorded a thick slither of limestone rubble beneath the cliff face.

senses.definition: A group of snakes.
senses.example: We spotted a slither of snakes sunning themselves on the warm flat stones.

core.definition: To move along the ground or over a surface with a smooth, sliding, winding motion, like a snake.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SLITH-er. The 'th' is voiced, as in 'this' and 'other', not the unvoiced 'th' of 'think'. The final -er is a light, rhotic syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can be creepy or sinister, especially for people who sneak away or evade responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use slither most often for snakes, and also for anything that moves in a winding, sliding way, like a lizard, a rope or a stream. It is also used figuratively, as in 'he slithered out of the meeting', to suggest someone slipped away to avoid trouble. In casual talk, slither is vivid but mildly dramatic.

distinctions.note: Slide is a smooth movement along a surface, while slither suggests a winding, snake-like motion.
Slink means to move stealthily, often out of shame or guilt, while slither focuses on the sliding, winding movement.
Slip means to lose footing or move quickly and often accidentally, while slither is a deliberate, sinuous motion.

examples.everyday: A garter snake slithered across the trail right in front of us.
examples.professional: He slithered out of the meeting before anyone could ask him about the missed deadline.
examples.analytical: The politician's answers slithered between positions, never committing to a claim that could be tested.

nuance.analogy: Like a ribbon of water running down a windowpane, always finding a way around.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English slidren, from Old English slidrian, a frequentative of slidan, 'to slide'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'th' as a 't' or 's' (SLIT-er or SLIS-er) instead of a voiced 'th'.
Using slither for ordinary walking or sliding across a floor in a neutral context, where slide or slip is more natural.

slither.etymology: From Middle English *slitheren*, alteration of *slideren* (“to slither, creep”), from Old English *slidrian* (“to slip, slide, slither”), from **slidrōn* (“to slide, slither”), from Proto-Indo-European **h₃sleydʰ-* (“to slip”), equivalent to *slide* + *-er*.

senses.definition: A very light state of sleep, almost awake.
senses.example: She drifted in a light slumber, half aware of the television murmuring downstairs.

senses.definition: A very heavy state of sleep.
senses.example: After the long shift, he fell into a deep slumber and didn't hear the alarm.

senses.definition: A state of ignorance or inaction.
senses.example: The town had sunk into a slumber, its shops closed and its council idle for years.

senses.definition: (rare) The snooze button on an alarm clock.
senses.example: He hit slumber on his alarm clock three times before finally getting out of bed.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To be in a very light state of sleep, almost awake.
senses.example: The old dog slumbers by the fireplace every afternoon, undisturbed by visitors.

senses.definition: To be inactive or negligent.
senses.example: For years the city slumbered while its neighbors invested in new transit.

core.definition: A deep, quiet sleep, often used in literary or gentle contexts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The b is silent in careful speech before a vowel, but the mb is often pronounced as m with a faint b, so keep the sound brief.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to gentle. It sounds soft and poetic, and it is often used for peaceful or deep sleep.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say sleep in everyday speech; slumber sounds literary or gentle, as in a lullaby or a bedtime story. You might hear slumber party for a sleepover, which is a common phrase for children and teens. Using the word in ordinary conversation may sound a bit quaint.

distinctions.note: Sleep is the everyday word; slumber is more literary or gentle and suggests deep, peaceful rest.
A nap is a short daytime sleep, while slumber can be a long, deep sleep.

examples.everyday: Did the kids finally fall into a deep slumber after the story?
examples.professional: The server was in a slumber mode overnight to save energy, so the first request in the morning was slow.
examples.analytical: The poet treats slumber as a threshold where the self is briefly stripped of its daytime anxieties.

nuance.analogy: Slumber is like a quiet lake under a still sky: calm, deep, and hard to disturb.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English slumberen, related to slumber as a frequentative of sleep-related Old English roots.
common_mistakes: Using slumber in everyday speech where sleep is more natural.
Pronouncing the b clearly in SLUM-ber-ing, which sounds unnatural to most Americans.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the idea of slumber often appears where God is contrasted with human weakness. The Hebrew verb num (נוּם) means to slumber or doze. Psalm 121:3-4 says that the one who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep, emphasizing God's constant watch. Proverbs 6:9-10 uses the image of the sluggard who loves a little sleep, a little slumber, and so invites poverty.

slumber.etymology: From Middle English *slombren*, *slomren*, frequentative of Middle English *slummen*, *slumen* (“to doze”), probably from Middle English *slume* (“slumber”), from Old English *slūma*, from Proto-Germanic **slūm-* (“slack, loose, limp, flabby”), from…

senses.definition: Containing a large amount of smoke, especially from cigarettes.
senses.example: The smoke-filled bar made my eyes sting, so we stepped outside for fresh air.

core.definition: Full of smoke, often thick cigarette or cigar smoke, so that it is hard to see or breathe comfortably.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FILLED, the second word, while SMOKE gets a lighter stress. Do not add an extra vowel between the l and d at the end, and remember the final d is a clear sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It usually describes an unpleasant environment, such as a room, bar or car, and it can suggest poor air quality or an old-fashioned atmosphere.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use smoke-filled to describe rooms, bars, or vehicles where many people have been smoking. In the US smoking is banned in most indoor public places, so the word now often sounds like a description of the past or of a place that has not been cleaned up. It is also used figuratively, as in a smoke-filled room for political deal making.

distinctions.note: Smoky describes something that has a lot of smoke or a smoke-like quality, while smoke-filled emphasizes that a space is full of smoke.
Smoke-free means smoking is not allowed, while smoke-filled describes the actual condition of the air.

examples.everyday: Grandpa's old truck always felt smoke-filled, even after we opened all the windows.
examples.professional: The client asked us to check whether the older hotel rooms were still smoke-filled from before the building went smoke-free.
examples.analytical: The phrase smoke-filled room has come to symbolize backroom political deals, although the image rests on a historical atmosphere that has largely vanished.

nuance.analogy: A smoke-filled room is like a fog bank you can taste, where you can barely see across the room.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing smoke-filled as SMOKE-filled with equal stress on both parts, when the stress is usually on FILLED.
Using smoke-filled to mean smoky in a general sense of smell, when the word refers to a space that is full of smoke.

senses.definition: In a snobbish manner.

core.definition: In a way that shows you look down on people you think are less refined, educated, or important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ly is a light 'lee' with a short vowel, not the sound of 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes an action or tone of superiority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use snobbishly to describe how someone speaks or acts, as in 'She snobbishly declined the paper cup.' It is less common in casual speech than snobby, but it sounds natural in writing and in describing behavior. Use it to criticize an action rather than to label a whole person.

distinctions.note: Haughtily stresses arrogant pride; snobbishly stresses looking down on people by status, taste, or background.
Condescendingly suggests talking down to someone as if they are less capable; snobbishly is about superiority in taste or class.

examples.everyday: The host smiled snobbishly when I asked whether the wine came in a box.
examples.professional: She snobbishly dismissed the junior analyst's model without even reading the code.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that critics too often judge popular art snobbishly, mistaking unfamiliarity for low quality.

nuance.analogy: Like raising an eyebrow before you have even taken a bite.
nuance.etymology: From snobbish plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Dropping one b and writing snobishly.
Using snobbishly to describe a person's identity; say 'he is a snob' or 'he is snobby', and use snobbishly for how he acts.

senses.definition: Having a lot of things to do, usually work-related; tied up.
senses.example: We are completely snowed under at work because it is the end of the tax year.

core.definition: Overwhelmed with a large amount of work or responsibilities; buried in tasks.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on UN in under, and make the final syllable a relaxed, r-colored schwa. The -ed in snowed is a plain d sound, so do not add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative, implying stress and overload, but often said in a humorous or sympathetic way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in workplace talk and casual conversation, usually in the passive: 'I'm snowed under this week.' It is informal, so it suits coworkers and friends more than formal letters. A natural reply is 'Oh no, hang in there' or 'Let me know if I can help.'

distinctions.note: Swamped is a bit stronger and more common for any heavy overload, while snowed under is a lighter, more colorful way to say you have too much to do.

examples.everyday: Sorry I missed your call, I'm snowed under with the kids' schedules this week.
examples.professional: I'm snowed under with the model review, so can we move the planning meeting to Thursday?
examples.analytical: Researchers who are snowed under by administrative tasks often have less time for careful reflection on their methods.

nuance.analogy: Like a car buried by a heavy snowfall, you cannot move until someone clears a path.
nuance.etymology: From the image of being buried under a heavy snowfall, used figuratively for being overwhelmed.
common_mistakes: Using snowed under for an actual snowfall in everyday speech; it is figurative for having too much to do.
Saying I am snowed with work; the usual phrase is snowed under with work.

senses.definition: A method of teaching through questions rather than lectures.
senses.example: Our philosophy professor uses the Socratic method, asking pointed questions until we discover our own contradictions.

core.definition: A teaching method that uses a series of questions to lead students to discover ideas and test their beliefs for themselves.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the 'KRAT' in Socratic and the 'METH' in method. The final syllable of 'method' is weak, so it sounds like 'uhd' and not 'odd'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests thoughtful teaching that builds critical thinking, though students may find it frustrating when the teacher will not give direct answers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in education, especially in law schools, where it is strongly associated with case-based classes in which professors call on students with questions. In conversation, people often say 'the Socratic method' when describing a teacher who answers questions with more questions. It is a formal term, but educated Americans use it casually as well.

distinctions.note: A Socratic seminar is a structured group discussion of a text, while the Socratic method is a broader teaching approach used by one instructor.
A lecture delivers information directly, while the Socratic method draws out understanding through questions.
Inquiry-based learning is a wider educational philosophy about student investigation, whereas the Socratic method specifically relies on dialogue and questioning.

examples.everyday: My nephew's teacher uses the Socratic method, so he never just gives the answer and makes the kids think it through.
examples.professional: I'm trying the Socratic method in our onboarding sessions by asking new analysts to explain their own assumptions.
examples.analytical: Plato's dialogues present the Socratic method as a way to test beliefs through a chain of carefully chosen questions.

nuance.analogy: It is like a coach who makes you find your own mistake on the film instead of telling you what it was.
nuance.etymology: Named after Socrates (Greek Sōkratēs); method comes from Greek methodos, meaning a pursuit or inquiry.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in Socratic, which should be on 'KRAT'.
Assuming it simply means asking lots of questions, when it is a structured method aimed at reasoning.

socratic-method.etymology: Named for *Socrates*, who employs it in Plato's dialogues.

senses.definition: Appropriate to, or in the way of, a soldier.
senses.example: His soldierly demeanour stood him good stead in civilian life when vicissitudes would assail him.

senses.definition: In the manner of a soldier.
senses.example: He carried the heavy pack soldierly across the muddy field, never once complaining.

core.definition: Having the bearing, discipline, or courage expected of a soldier.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle er is a reduced rhotic vowel, and the final -ly is a light 'lee'. Do not add a separate d sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; suggests discipline, courage, and dignity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'soldierly' mostly in writing, speeches, or descriptions of posture and behavior, and it sounds formal. In everyday talk people say 'disciplined', 'military-style', or 'like a soldier'. The adverb sense exists but is rare, so say 'like a soldier' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Military' describes institutions, equipment, or operations; 'soldierly' describes personal qualities such as discipline and bearing.
'Martial' suggests war or a fighting spirit and is often literary; 'soldierly' focuses on the conduct and character of a soldier.
'Soldierlike' is more casual and describes appearance or manner; 'soldierly' is more formal and suggests an admirable quality.

examples.everyday: My grandpa stood with a soldierly posture even in his eighties.
examples.professional: The new team lead has a soldierly sense of discipline that keeps our sprints on schedule.
examples.analytical: The author's account of the general's soldierly courage reflects an older ideal of honor that modern readers may find distant.

nuance.analogy: Soldierly discipline is like a well-tuned orchestra, where every player keeps time even under pressure.
nuance.etymology: From 'soldier' plus the suffix -ly, meaning in the manner of a soldier.
common_mistakes: Saying 'soldierly' with a separate d sound, as in 'SOHL-dee-er-lee'.
Using 'soldierly' to mean 'military' in technical contexts, where 'military' is the normal word.
Confusing 'soldierly' with 'soldiery', which means a group of soldiers.

senses.definition: To find an answer or solution to a problem or question; to work out.
To find out the perpetrator, the motive etc.
senses.example: to solve a murder to solve a crime

senses.definition: To find the values of variables that satisfy a system of equations and/or inequalities.
senses.example: Our statistics team needs to solve the system of equations before the model runs.

senses.definition: To algebraically manipulate an equation or inequality into a form that isolates a chosen variable on one side, so that the other side consists of an expression that may be used to generate solutions.
senses.example: To solve for the learning rate, first rearrange the formula so that it isolates alpha.

senses.definition: To loosen or separate the parts of. To dissolve.
senses.example: The acid began to solve the limestone, loosening its crumbly parts in the water.

senses.definition: (rare) A solution; an explanation.
senses.example: Today's cryptic crossword was an easy solve.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To find the answer or solution to a problem, question or puzzle.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with the stress on SAHLV. The final e is silent, so end on the v with no extra vowel after it. The vowel is the open ah sound of cot.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes successful problem-solving and is generally admired.
nuance.usage_note: Solve is used everywhere in American English, from math class to workplace discussion to crime shows. In casual speech Americans often say figure out or work out instead, as in let's figure this out. Solve sounds natural with problems, puzzles, crimes and equations.

distinctions.note: Solve is used for problems and puzzles, while resolve is used for conflicts, disputes and disagreements that get settled.
Figure out is more informal and often means understanding something, while solve implies reaching a definite answer to a problem.

examples.everyday: Can you help me solve this crossword clue? I have been stuck on it all morning.
examples.professional: Let's solve this bug before the Friday release so we don't have to delay the whole team.
examples.analytical: Kant argued that some metaphysical questions cannot be solved by reason alone, because reason goes beyond what experience can test.

nuance.analogy: A solution is like a key that turns the lock, and solving is the act of finding the right key.
nuance.etymology: From Latin solvere, to loosen or release.
common_mistakes: Adding a vowel after the l, saying suh-LOHV-ih or sow-lve, instead of a single syllable.
Using solve about, as in solve about the problem, instead of solve the problem.

senses.definition: On some occasions, over some periods, or in certain circumstances, but not always.
senses.example: Sometimes I sit and think, but mostly I just sit.

core.definition: On some occasions or in certain circumstances, but not always.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -s is voiced like a z, so it sounds like SUM-tymz. Do not add an extra syllable such as 'sum-TIME-us'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes frequency and carries no praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sometimes constantly in everyday speech, either before the verb ('I sometimes forget') or at the start of a sentence ('Sometimes I forget'). It suits any setting and never sounds rude. For a softer or more casual tone, speakers often say 'every once in a while' or 'every now and then'.

distinctions.note: Sometime (one word) means at an unspecified point in the past or future, as in 'Let's meet sometime next week', while sometimes means on certain occasions.
Occasionally implies infrequent, irregular events and sounds a bit more formal; sometimes is more neutral and conversational.

examples.everyday: Sometimes I walk to work, but today I drove because it was raining.
examples.professional: Sometimes the model passes validation but still fails on the holdout set, so we test it another way.
examples.analytical: Sometimes people treat faith and doubt as opposites, though many thinkers see them as bound together in practice.

nuance.analogy: Like a porch light that comes on only on certain nights.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English sum tymes, from some plus time, with the -s as an adverbial genitive ending.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words ('some times') when you mean 'on certain occasions'; the one-word form is standard in that sense.
Confusing it with 'sometime', which refers to an unspecified time ('We should talk sometime').

sometimes.etymology: From Middle English *sumtymes*, *somtymes*, *som tymes*, equivalent to *sometime* + *-s*.

senses.definition: A writer of sonnets or small poems.
To compose sonnets.

core.definition: A poet who writes sonnets, or a writer of short, rhyming poems in the sonnet form.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the last syllable, TEER, and the middle syllable is a weak uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can imply a minor or overly precious poet when used dismissively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sonneteer mainly in literary criticism, teaching, and history of poetry, rarely in casual talk. Calling someone a sonneteer usually points to their main form, the sonnet. Depending on tone, it can suggest the poet is skilled but minor.

distinctions.note: Poet is the general term, while sonneteer specifically names a writer whose main form is the sonnet.
A lyricist writes words for songs, while a sonneteer writes fourteen-line poems usually not meant for music.
Versifier is a dismissive word for someone who writes verse without much originality, while sonneteer is neutral.

examples.professional: The publisher wants a sonneteer for the anthology, so we need someone who can keep fourteen lines tight.
examples.analytical: Petrarch and Shakespeare are the sonneteers most often compared in critical studies of love poetry.

nuance.analogy: A sonneteer is to the sonnet what a sculptor is to marble: the form is fixed, and the craft lies in shaping it.
nuance.etymology: From sonnet (from Italian sonetto, a little song) plus -eer.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on the first syllable, as in SON-ih-teer, instead of the final syllable.
Confusing sonneteer with sonnet, which is stressed on the first syllable.

senses.definition: Of a person: having obtained worldly experience, and lacking naiveté; cosmopolitan, worldly-wise.
senses.example: Growing up in Paris made her far more sophisticated than the kids in our small town.

senses.definition: Of art or other things: appealing to the tastes of an intellectual or sophisticated (sense 1) person; cerebral; also, cultured, elegant, refined.
senses.example: The film's sophisticated score rewards viewers who listen closely to its layered harmonies.

senses.definition: Complicated, especially of complex technology.
senses.example: The new hospital scanner is far more sophisticated than anything we used before.

senses.definition: Mixed with a foreign or inferior substance; not genuine or pure; unrefined, adulterated, impure.
senses.example: The chemist warned that the honey had been sophisticated with corn syrup.

senses.definition: Of a thing: having its meaning changed in a deceptive or misleading way.
senses.example: The report's sophisticated accounting made the losses look like profits to investors.

core.definition: Having worldly experience, good taste, and polished manners; or, of things, complex and refined in design or thought.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FIS, the second syllable. Many learners insert an extra schwa or say an /ə/ in the middle, so keep it as sih-FIS-tih-KAY-tid with a clear short i in the first syllable and a reduced vowel in the last.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises refinement and worldliness, though it can sound slightly skeptical when describing a person who seems too slick. For technology, it means complex and advanced, which is also positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to compliment someone's taste or style, as in a sophisticated restaurant or a sophisticated audience. It also describes sophisticated software or equipment, meaning highly complex. Calling a young child sophisticated would sound like a joke or a compliment on maturity. Natural replies are simply 'Thanks' or 'It's pretty sophisticated, isn't it?'

distinctions.note: Complex describes having many interrelated parts; sophisticated adds the sense of refined skill or worldly polish.
Elegant focuses on graceful beauty of appearance or design, while sophisticated focuses on knowledge, judgment, and worldliness.

examples.everyday: My sister has really sophisticated taste in wine, so I let her pick the bottle.
examples.professional: Our new fraud model uses a sophisticated ensemble of gradient-boosted trees and a neural network.
examples.analytical: Hume's account of causation is more sophisticated than the simple regularity view it is often reduced to.

nuance.analogy: A sophisticated person is like a well-tailored suit: the quality shows in details that a casual observer may not name.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin sophisticare, to adulterate, from Greek sophistēs, a wise man or sophist.
common_mistakes: Using it for simple or cheap things, when the word implies refinement or complexity.
Pronouncing it as sof-iss-tih-KAY-tid, moving the stress to the wrong syllable.

senses.definition: Human-readable instructions in a programming language, to be transformed into machine instructions by a compiler, assembler or other translator, or to be carried out directly by an interpreter.

core.definition: Human-readable instructions written in a programming language, which a compiler, assembler or interpreter later turns into machine instructions.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on CODE, with a lighter secondary stress on source. Keep the r in both words and say the vowel in source as aw, not oo.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers in the US use source code daily in code reviews, repositories and documentation. People say 'open-source' for code that is publicly available, and 'push your code' or 'commit the source' for sharing changes. Outside technology, the phrase is rarely used, so explain it if you use it with non-programmers.

distinctions.note: Machine code is the binary instructions that the processor runs directly. Source code is written for people to read and edit first.
Object code is the compiled output of source code, produced before linking. Source code is the human-written version.
An executable is a runnable program produced from source code. Source code is what you write and read.

examples.everyday: My brother is a programmer, and he showed me his source code, but I couldn't follow any of it.
examples.professional: Can you push the latest source code to the shared repo before the review this afternoon?
examples.analytical: Whether a program's meaning resides in its source code or in its observable behavior is a question the philosophy of software keeps returning to.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe written in a language you can read, before the cook turns it into a finished meal.
nuance.etymology: Source is from Old French sourse, from Latin surgere, to rise; code is from Latin codex, meaning a block of wood or a book.
common_mistakes: Writing it as one word, sourcecode, or with a hyphen in formal documents; the standard form is two words.
Confusing source code with machine code; source code is readable by people, but machine code is not.

senses.definition: The direction towards the pole to the right-hand side of someone facing east, specifically 180°, or (on another celestial object) the direction towards the pole lying on the southern side of the invariable plane.
senses.example: Germany is south of Denmark.

senses.definition: The southern region or area; the inhabitants thereof.
In a church: the direction to the right-hand side of a person facing the altar.
senses.example: The stained glass window in the south of the nave shows Saint Peter.

senses.definition: The negative or south pole of a magnet.
senses.example: The south of one magnet attracts the north of another magnet.

senses.definition: Toward the south; southward.
senses.example: The geese flew south for the winter, following the river valley.

senses.definition: From the south.
senses.example: A south wind brought warm humid air up from the Gulf of Mexico.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the south; southern.
senses.example: The south coast of England is famous for its chalk cliffs and beaches.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the part of a corridor used by southbound traffic.
senses.example: south highway 1

senses.definition: Designating, or situated in, the liturgical south.
senses.example: The south aisle of the cathedral contains the chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary.

senses.definition: Toward the south; southward.
senses.example: The geese flew south for the winter, following the river valley.

senses.definition: Downward.
senses.example: Her bank balance headed south after the rent check cleared.

senses.definition: In an adverse direction or trend.
senses.example: His fortunes have been going south ever since he was tricked into investing in that ostrich farm.

senses.definition: Of wind, from the south.
senses.example: The wind blew south all afternoon, bringing humid air and thunderstorms.

senses.definition: To turn or move toward the south; to veer toward the south.
senses.example: Over the afternoon, the storm front souths toward the coast.

senses.definition: To come to the meridian; to cross the north and south line.
senses.example: The moon souths at nine.

core.definition: The direction opposite north, on your right when you face east; also the southern part of an area or region.

pronunciation.tip: The 'th' is voiceless, as in 'thin', so do not voice it into a 'z' or 'd' sound. The vowel is the 'ow' of 'mouth', so say 'sowth', not 'sooth'.
